blocks.x: Here is a story one letter cannot carry. Lena scored 53 points on a quiz made of 2-point and 5-point questions, and she does not know the split. With \(a\) correct 2-point answers and \(b\) correct 5-point answers, her fact reads \(2a+5b=53\). No value of \(a\) can be checked on its own. The claim involves both letters at once.

Four pairs are proposed for \(2a+5b=53\), each written with \(a\) first and \(b\) second. $$(24,1)\qquad(19,3)\qquad(9,7)\qquad(11,6)$$ Substitute both values from each pair and evaluate the left side. Enter how many of the four pairs make the claim true.
hints: Each pair gets the full check from 4.1. Replace \(a\) and \(b\) with the pair's two values, evaluate the left side, and compare it with \(53\).
The last pair gives \(2(11)+5(6)=22+30\). Settle whether that is \(53\), then run the other three the same way.
blocks.sol: The first three pairs pass, \(48+5=53\), \(38+15=53\), and \(18+35=53\), while \((11,6)\) gives \(22+30=52\). So \(\boxed{3}\) of the four pairs make the claim true. Three different pairs already satisfy the same equation, and nothing in it stops more.

blocks.x: A solution is a pair. An equation in two variables makes a claim about two numbers at once. A solution is a pair of values, one for each variable, that makes the claim true. Checking a candidate substitutes both values and evaluates each side, 4.1's check with two substitutions instead of one. The pair records which value belongs to which letter, so \((24,1)\) means \(a=24\) and \(b=1\), and the order matters. One number alone is not a solution, because the claim cannot even be tested until both letters have values.
The pair \(x=12,\ y=2\) solves \(4x+9y=66\), since \(48+18=66\). Now swap the two values. Substitute \(x=2,\ y=12\) and enter the value the left side takes.
hints: A pair says which value belongs to which letter, so the swapped version is a different pair making a different substitution.
With \(x=2\) and \(y=12\), the first term is \(4(2)=8\) and the second is \(9(12)\).
blocks.sol: With \(x=2\) and \(y=12\), the left side is \(4(2)+9(12)=8+108=\boxed{116}\). That is not 66, so the swapped pair fails. A pair carries its order, and \((12,2)\) and \((2,12)\) are different candidates.

blocks.x: Checking given pairs is one skill. Producing your own is the next. Choose a value for one variable and the equation collapses to one variable, which 4.2 solves. In Lena's equation, \(a=14\) gives \(28+5b=53\), so \(5b=25\) and \(b=5\), the pair \((14,5)\). The story allows only whole counts, but the equation is its own object and takes any number.
The equation \(x+2y=49\) has a solution pair with \(x=17\). Substitute that value, solve the equation that remains, and enter \(y\).
hints: Substituting the given \(x\) leaves an equation in \(y\) alone, exactly the kind 4.2 solves.
After the substitution the claim reads \(17+2y=49\). Solve \(2y=32\).
blocks.sol: Substituting \(x=17\) gives \(17+2y=49\), so \(2y=32\) and \(y=\boxed{16}\). The pair \((17,16)\) checks, \(17+32=49\).

blocks.x: The equation \(6x+y=42\) has a solution pair with \(x=10\). Substitute the given value, solve for the partner, and enter \(y\).
hints: Replace \(x\) with \(10\) and compute \(6x\) first. It is fine if that value comes out larger than \(42\).
Substituting gives \(60+y=42\). Since \(60\) is already more than \(42\), \(y\) must be negative.
blocks.sol: Substituting \(x=10\) gives \(60+y=42\), so \(y=42-60=\boxed{-18}\). The check passes, \(60+(-18)=42\). A solution pair can include a negative number.

blocks.x: The equation \(3x+10y=58\) has a solution pair with \(x=18\). Find the partner value and enter \(y\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The collapsed equation is 4.2 work, and nothing promises a whole-number answer.
Substituting gives \(54+10y=58\). Solve \(10y=4\), then reduce.
blocks.sol: Substituting \(x=18\) gives \(54+10y=58\), so \(10y=4\) and \(y=\frac{4}{10}=\boxed{\tfrac{2}{5}}\). Nothing restricts pairs to whole numbers. Every choice of \(x\), whole or not, gets a partner.

blocks.x: One equation, many solutions. Every value chosen for \(x\) collapses a two-variable equation into a one-variable equation, and 4.2 finds the partner \(y\). A different \(x\) gives a different pair, so the supply of solutions never runs out, and the pairs come whole, negative, and fractional. The consequence is that one equation in two variables cannot pin down its pair. Solving it cannot mean finding the solution, because there is no single solution to find.

Around 250 CE, Diophantus of Alexandria filled his Arithmetica with problems that have more unknowns than equations, so endless solutions fit. He was content to find one. Equations like these are still called Diophantine in his honor.

Two secret numbers satisfy \(x+y=101\). Finding them looks hopeless, since pairs passing that test can be listed all day and every one of them keeps the secret. Suppose a second fact about the same two numbers turns up. It is worth asking what one more fact could possibly change.

All four of these pairs satisfy \(x+y=101\). $$(98,3)\qquad(93,8)\qquad(79,22)\qquad(70,31)$$ Now the second fact arrives. The same two numbers also satisfy \(x-y=39\). Enter how many of the four pairs satisfy both facts.
hints: Each pair already passes the first fact, so only the new claim needs testing.
The first pair gives \(98-3=95\), not \(39\). Keep going down the list.
blocks.sol: The differences are \(98-3=95\), \(93-8=85\), \(79-22=57\), and \(70-31=39\). Only \((70,31)\) gives \(39\), so \(\boxed{1}\) pair satisfies both facts. The first fact allowed an endless list, and the second fact cut it to one pair.

blocks.x: A system of equations. A set of equations about the same variables, all required to hold at once, is called a system of equations. A solution of a system is a pair that satisfies every equation in it, and a pair that fails even one equation is not a solution, no matter how many of the others it satisfies. This is why a second equation has power. Each equation alone allows endless pairs, but few pairs pass every test, and often the count is exactly one.

Lena knew one more fact all along. The quiz had 13 questions, so \(a+b=13\) must also hold. Of every pair passing \(2a+5b=53\), only \((4,9)\) passes both, since \(8+45=53\) and \(4+9=13\). She got four 2-point questions and nine 5-point questions. Checking a pair against a system means checking it against every equation in it.

For the system \(2u+v=69\) and \(u+v=37\), test the pairs \((30,9)\), \((32,5)\), and \((26,11)\). One satisfies only the first equation, one satisfies only the second, and one satisfies both. Enter \(u\) for the solution of the system.
hints: A solution of a system passes every equation in it. A pair that fails one check is not a solution, even if it passes every other.
\((30,9)\) makes the first equation true, since \(60+9=69\). Check it in the second before deciding anything.
blocks.sol: \((30,9)\) gives \(60+9=69\) but \(30+9=39\), not \(37\). \((26,11)\) gives \(26+11=37\) but \(52+11=63\), not \(69\). \((32,5)\) gives \(64+5=69\) and \(32+5=37\), so it passes both and \(u=\boxed{32}\). Each rejected pair passed exactly one equation, and one pass is worth nothing in a system.

blocks.x: Both \((13,7)\) and \((29,3)\) satisfy \(x+4y=41\). Only one of them also satisfies \(2x-y=19\). Enter \(x+y\) for the solution of the system.
hints: Passing the first equation is not enough. Run each pair through the second and keep the one that passes.
For \((29,3)\), the left side of the second equation is \(58-3\). Compare that with \(19\).

blocks.x: How is that single pair found when no candidates are given? For now, by search. Take the friendlier equation, list whole-number pairs that satisfy it, and test each one in the other equation until a pair passes both. This works when the numbers are kind, and it fails the moment they are not. Lessons 5.2 and 5.3 build methods that always work.
Two numbers satisfy \(x+y=23\) and \(5x-y=25\). List whole-number pairs from the first equation and test them in the second until one passes. Enter \(x\).
hints: Every candidate from the first fact has the form \(x\) and \(23-x\), so each choice of \(x\) names a full pair to test.
If a test comes out below \(25\), raise \(x\) and try again. The value of \(5x-y\) climbs quickly as \(x\) grows, so the search stays short.
blocks.sol: Candidates from the first equation include \((7,16)\), \((8,15)\), and \((9,14)\). Testing \((8,15)\) in the second, \(5(8)-15=40-15=25\), so both facts hold and \(x=\boxed{8}\). Raising \(x\) by \(1\) raises \(5x-y\) by \(6\), so the second equation is hit exactly once.

blocks.x: The system \(m+n=67\) and \(m+n=73\) makes two claims about the same two numbers. Take any pair satisfying the first equation, test it in the second, and enter the number of solutions of the system.
hints: Read the two claims side by side. Both are about the sum of the same two numbers.
A pair with \(m+n=67\) makes the second left side \(67\), and \(67\) is not \(73\).
blocks.sol: Any pair passing the first equation has \(m+n=67\), so in the second equation its left side is \(67\), never \(73\). No pair passes both, and the system has \(\boxed{0}\) solutions. Two claims about the same numbers can simply contradict each other. Chapter 7 will draw what that looks like.

blocks.x: What a system can have. Usually a second fact pins the pair down and the system has exactly one solution. Sometimes the two claims conflict, as \(m+n=67\) and \(m+n=73\) do, and the system has no solution at all. Testing settles any pair somebody names, but it cannot produce a pair from nothing, and searching works only while the numbers are kind. Closing that gap, finding the pair instead of confirming it, is this chapter's work.
Two numbers satisfy \(x+y=6\) and \(x-y=14\). Search pairs from the first fact, and do not stop at positive candidates. Enter \(y\).
hints: The difference \(14\) is larger than the sum \(6\). Two positive numbers always differ by less than their sum, so one member must be negative.
Pairs summing to 6 include ones with a negative member, like \(9\) and \(-3\).
blocks.sol: Pairs from the first fact run \((7,-1)\), \((8,-2)\), \((9,-3)\), \((10,-4)\). Testing \((10,-4)\) in the second, \(10-(-4)=14\), so both facts hold and \(y=\boxed{-4}\). Positive pairs summing to \(6\) differ by less than \(6\), so the pair that works has to include a negative member.

blocks.x: A system is two claims sharing one pair. Testing confirms a pair, and searching finds one while the numbers stay kind, but they will not stay kind. Lesson 5.2, Substitution, turns two equations in two variables into one equation in one variable, chapter 4's home ground.

review.x: Substitute the pair \(x=11,\ y=2\) into \(8x+3y=94\) and evaluate the left side. It matches the right side. Enter the number both sides equal.
hints: A pair substitutes both letters at once, each value into its own letter.
The first term is \(8\cdot 11\). Add \(3\cdot 2\) to it.
review.sol: The left side is \(8(11)+3(2)=88+6=\boxed{94}\). One check settles a pair, both values go in together and the two sides are compared once.

review.x: The pair \((7,6)\) is claimed to solve \(9x+4y=91\). Substitute \(x=7,\ y=6\) and enter the value the left side actually takes.
hints: A failed check still ends with a number. Report whatever the left side works out to, even if it does not match the right side.
Substituting gives the two terms \(9(7)\) and \(4(6)\). Compute each product, then add.
review.sol: \(9(7)+4(6)=63+24=\boxed{87}\). That is not \(91\), so \((7,6)\) is not a solution. A check either matches the right side or it does not, and this one misses by \(4\).

review.x: The equation \(7x+y=86\) has a solution pair with \(x=11\). Substitute that value and solve for the letter that remains. Enter \(y\).
hints: Substituting the given \(x\) collapses the claim to a one-variable equation, a 4.2 solve.
After substituting, the equation reads \(77+y=86\).
review.sol: Substituting \(x=11\) gives \(77+y=86\), so \(y=\boxed{9}\). Check, \(7(11)+9=77+9=86\), and the pair \((11,9)\) passes.

review.x: The equation \(x-2y=11\) has a solution pair with \(y=12\). Enter \(x\).
hints: This time the given value fills the second slot. Substitute it and one letter remains.
Substituting \(y=12\) leaves \(x-24=11\).
review.sol: Substituting \(y=12\) gives \(x-24=11\), so \(x=\boxed{35}\). Check, \(35-2(12)=35-24=11\). Either member of the pair can be the given one.

review.x: Check the pairs \((6,0)\), \((4,6)\), \((3,8)\), \((5,2)\) against \(3x+y=18\), substituting \(x\) first and \(y\) second. Enter how many of the four are solutions.
hints: Each pair gets its own full check, both values in, then compare with \(18\).
The pair \((3,8)\) gives \(9+8\). Decide whether that is \(18\), then finish the list.
review.sol: The left sides are \(18+0=18\), \(12+6=18\), \(9+8=17\), \(15+2=17\), so \(\boxed{2}\) of the pairs are solutions. Zero is a legal value for a member of a pair, and \((6,0)\) passes like any other.

review.x: Substitute the pair \((24,9)\) into \(x+9y=4x+y\), evaluating each side separately. Both sides come out to the same number. Enter it.
hints: A variable can sit on both sides. The check does not change, evaluate each side and compare.
The left side is \(24+9(9)\). The right side is \(4(24)+9\).
review.sol: The left side is \(24+81=105\) and the right side is \(96+9=105\), so both sides equal \(\boxed{105}\). The pair checks against the whole claim at once, whichever side each letter appears on.

review.x: The equation \(8x+y=50\) has a solution pair with \(x=9\). Enter \(y\).
hints: Nothing stops the chosen \(x\) from pushing the first term past \(50\).
Substituting gives \(72+y=50\), so \(y\) must undo the extra.
review.sol: Substituting \(x=9\) gives \(72+y=50\), so \(y=50-72=\boxed{-22}\). Check, \(8(9)+(-22)=72-22=50\). The pair has a negative member, and the check passes all the same.

review.x: The equation \(8x+6y=85\) has a solution pair with \(x=8\). Enter \(y\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Substitute the given \(x\) and solve what remains. Nothing requires the answer to be whole.
Substituting gives \(64+6y=85\), so \(6y=21\). Reduce the fraction.
review.sol: Substituting \(x=8\) gives \(64+6y=85\), so \(6y=21\) and \(y=\frac{21}{6}=\boxed{\frac{7}{2}}\). Check, \(64+6\cdot\frac{7}{2}=64+21=85\). Nothing in the equation forces \(y\) to be a whole number.

review.x: The equation \(4y-3x=21\) has a solution pair with \(x=9\). Enter \(y\).
hints: The known letter sits in the subtracted term this time. Substitute it and a one-variable equation remains.
Substituting gives \(4y-27=21\), a two-step solve.

review.x: Every pair solving \(x+5y=88\) also solves \(3x+15y=264\), since the second equation is the first with both sides multiplied by \(3\). The second fact adds nothing new. Enter \(y\) for the pair with \(x=13\).
hints: Only one genuinely different claim is in play, so work with the friendlier one.
In \(x+5y=88\), substituting \(x=13\) leaves \(5y=75\).
review.sol: Using the first equation, \(13+5y=88\), so \(5y=75\) and \(y=\boxed{15}\). Check in the second, \(3(13)+15(15)=39+225=264\). A second equation only pins the pair when it says something the first did not.

review.x: All four of \((35,11)\), \((37,7)\), \((39,3)\), \((28,25)\) satisfy \(2x+y=81\). Exactly one also satisfies \(3x-y=104\). Enter \(x\) for that pair.
hints: The first equation is already settled for every pair, so only the second needs testing.
For \((35,11)\) the second left side is \(105-11\). Work down the list.
review.sol: Testing the second equation, \(105-11=94\), \(111-7=104\), \(117-3=114\), \(84-25=59\). Only \((37,7)\) passes both, so \(x=\boxed{37}\). A solution of a system must satisfy every equation, and failing even one rules a pair out.

review.x: Two numbers add to \(87\) and differ by \(33\). Enter the larger number.
hints: Write the two facts as a system, \(x+y=87\) and \(x-y=33\), then search pairs from the sum.
A pair like \(50\) and \(37\) sums right but differs by only \(13\). Push the two numbers further apart.
review.sol: The facts are \(x+y=87\) and \(x-y=33\). Searching pairs that sum to \(87\), the pair \((60,27)\) gives \(60-27=33\), so the larger number is \(\boxed{60}\). Check, \(60+27=87\).

review.x: Two numbers satisfy \(x+y=29\) and \(4x+y=71\). Test whole-number pairs from the first equation in the second until one passes, then enter the product \(xy\).
hints: Every candidate from the first fact has \(y=29-x\), so only \(x\) needs choosing.
Small \(x\) leaves \(4x+y\) well under \(71\). Start the search around \(x=13\) or \(14\).
review.sol: The pair \((14,15)\) sums to \(29\), and \(4(14)+15=56+15=71\) passes the second equation. So \(xy=14\cdot 15=\boxed{210}\). No other whole pair works, since raising \(x\) by \(1\) raises \(4x+y\) by \(3\), so \(71\) is hit exactly once.

review.x: For the system \(x+y=102\) and \(x+y=89\), any pair satisfying the first equation misses the second by one fixed amount. Enter that amount.
hints: Read the two claims side by side. Both are about the same left side.
A pair summing to \(102\) makes the second left side \(102\), not \(89\).
review.sol: Any pair with \(x+y=102\) makes the second equation read \(102=89\), which misses by \(102-89=\boxed{13}\). The two claims conflict for every pair at once, so this system has no solution.

review.x: The system \(x+y=112\) and \(x-y=112\) looks like the impossible kind, but the left sides differ, and it has exactly one solution. Enter \(x\).
hints: The sum and the difference of the pair are equal. Ask what \(y\) must be for that to happen.
Adding \(y\) and subtracting \(y\) give the same result only when \(y\) contributes nothing.
review.sol: If adding \(y\) and subtracting \(y\) leave the same value, then \(y=0\), and the first equation gives \(x=\boxed{112}\). Check, \(112+0=112\) and \(112-0=112\). Zero is a legal member of a pair, so the two claims agree instead of conflicting.

review.x: Two numbers satisfy \(m+n=5\) and \(m-n=17\). Search pairs from the first fact, and let the second number go negative. Enter \(n\).
hints: The difference is larger than the sum, so no pair of positive numbers can work.
Pairs summing to \(5\) include ones like \(9\) and \(-4\). Push until the difference reaches \(17\).
review.sol: The pair \((11,-6)\) gives \(11+(-6)=5\) and \(11-(-6)=11+6=17\), so \(n=\boxed{-6}\). A search that stops at positive candidates never finds this pair, since positive pairs summing to \(5\) differ by at most \(5\).

review.x: For one particular number \(k\), the pair \(x=16,\ y=-9\) is the solution of the system \(x+y=7\) and \(2x+5y=k\). Enter \(k\).
hints: This time the pair is known and part of the system is not. Substitute the pair into each equation and see what must be true.
The first equation checks, \(16+(-9)=7\). The second says \(k\) equals \(2(16)+5(-9)\).
review.sol: The first equation checks, \(16+(-9)=7\). Substituting the pair into the second, \(k=2(16)+5(-9)=32-45=\boxed{-13}\). Keep the parentheses, \(5(-9)\) is \(-45\), and the term joins the sum with its sign.

blocks.x: Two numbers satisfy \(y=3x+26\) and \(x+y=2\). Run 5.1's search on the second equation, \((0,2)\), \((1,1)\), \((2,0)\), and every candidate fails the first. The pair hides among negatives, where listing never ends. The first equation is not one more claim to test. It says what \(y\) is. At the solution, \(y\) and \(3x+26\) are the same number.
The first equation says \(y\) equals \(3x+26\), so write \(3x+26\) in \(y\)'s place in \(x+y=2\). One equation in one variable remains. Solve it and enter \(x\).
hints: The swap leaves an equation with only \(x\) in it, exactly the kind chapter 4 solves.
After the substitution the claim reads \(x+(3x+26)=2\). Collect the left side to \(4x+26=2\).
blocks.sol: \(x+(3x+26)=2\) collects to \(4x+26=2\), so \(4x=-24\) and \(x=\boxed{-6}\). The first equation names \(y\), so its expression can stand wherever \(y\) stands.

blocks.x: The partner is still missing. Substitute \(x=-6\) into \(y=3x+26\), the equation already solved for \(y\), and enter \(y\). Check the pair in both original equations first.
hints: The solved-form equation computes \(y\) from any \(x\), including this one.
Substituting gives \(y=3(-6)+26\). Keep the parentheses around the negative value.
blocks.sol: \(y=3(-6)+26=-18+26=\boxed{8}\). Check \((-6,8)\) in both originals, \(8=3(-6)+26\) and \(-6+8=2\), so the pair passes the full 5.1 test.

blocks.x: Substitution. When one equation gives a variable as an expression, replace that variable in the other equation with the expression. One variable remains, chapter 4 solves it, and back-substituting into the solved-form equation finds the partner. The swap is legal because at the solution pair the variable and its expression are the same number, the evaluating idea from 2.2, so the rewritten equation makes exactly the claim the old one made, equivalent in 4.2's sense.
The system \(x=3y+22\) and \(x+2y=112\) leads with \(x\) this time. Replace \(x\) in the second equation with \(3y+22\), solve for \(y\), back-substitute, and enter \(x\).
hints: Either letter can be the pre-solved one. The steps do not change. Replace the letter that equals an expression.
blocks.sol: \((3y+22)+2y=112\) gives \(5y+22=112\), so \(5y=90\), \(y=18\), and \(x=3(18)+22=\boxed{76}\). The ask is \(x\), so the back-substitution is not optional.

blocks.x: So far the replaced letter stood alone. In \(4x+3y=47\) the \(y\) is tripled, and \(3y\) means three copies of all of \(y\), so whatever stands in for \(y\) must arrive as one unit. With \(y=2x+7\), the incoming expression takes the seat as a block, not a piece at a time.

The tile lands as one unit, so parentheses close around it, \(4x+3(2x+7)=47\). Substituting a piece, or dropping the parentheses, writes a different equation.

Substitute in parentheses. Replacing the \(y\) of \(3y\) with \(2x+7\) must produce \(3(2x+7)\), which distributes by 2.1 to \(6x+21\). Written bare, \(4x+3\cdot 2x+7\) adds \(7\) where the faithful line adds \(21\), so every line after it is about a different equation, and the pair it lands on fails the original check. A coefficient slot means parentheses, no exceptions.
Solve the system \(y=3x-16\) and \(5x+2y=78\). The \(2y\) doubles the whole expression, so substitute in parentheses, distribute, and enter \(x+y\).
hints: Substitute the whole expression \(3x-16\) for \(y\) in the second equation, with parentheses around all of it.

blocks.x: A student substitutes \(y=2x-3\) into \(x+4y=51\) and writes \(x+4\cdot 2x-3=51\), no parentheses. That line gives \(x=6\), then \(y=9\), and the check fails, since \(6+4(9)=42\), not \(51\). Redo the substitution with the parentheses it needed and enter the correct \(x\).
hints: In \(4y\), the \(4\) must multiply everything \(y\) is, not just the first piece.
The faithful line is \(x+4(2x-3)=51\). Distribute, then collect.
blocks.sol: \(x+4(2x-3)=51\) gives \(9x-12=51\), so \(9x=63\) and \(x=\boxed{7}\), with \(y=2(7)-3=11\) and \(7+44=51\). The bare line subtracted \(3\) where the equation subtracts \(12\).

blocks.x: Nobody pre-solves equations for you outside a lesson. When neither equation arrives in solved form, pick a letter, solve for it with 4.3's moves, then substitute exactly as before. One isolate is the whole cost, and the rest of the run does not change.

Neither equation of \(3x+y=32\) and \(7x+2y=75\) is solved for a letter, but the first is one 4.3 move away. Solve it for \(y\), substitute into the second, and enter \(y\). Check the pair in both originals.
hints: Subtracting \(3x\) from both sides pre-solves the first equation for \(y\).
Substitute \(y=32-3x\) into the second equation to get \(7x+2(32-3x)=75\).

blocks.x: Choose the coefficient-1 letter. A letter with coefficient \(1\) or \(-1\) isolates without dividing, so the rest of the work has no fractions in it. Any choice is legal, and every choice gives the same solution pair. The only difference is the arithmetic, and cleaner arithmetic means fewer chances to slip, so scan both equations for a coefficient of \(1\) or \(-1\) before isolating anything.
In \(3x-y=20\) and \(5x+2y=4\) the \(y\) has coefficient \(-1\). Solving the first for \(y\) still takes one move, \(y=3x-20\). Substitute into the second equation and enter \(y\).
hints: Coefficient \(-1\) is as cheap as coefficient \(1\). No dividing happens on the way to solved form.
blocks.sol: \(5x+2(3x-20)=4\) gives \(11x-40=4\), so \(11x=44\), \(x=4\), and \(y=3(4)-20=\boxed{-8}\). Nothing stops a solution pair from being negative.

blocks.x: One letter in \(4x+y=198\) and \(2x+3y=204\) isolates without fractions. Find it, isolate it, substitute, solve the system, and enter the product \(xy\).
hints: Only \(y\) in the first equation has coefficient \(1\), so isolating it costs one 4.3 move and no fractions.
Substituting \(y=198-4x\) into the second equation gives \(2x+3(198-4x)=204\).

blocks.x: Babylonian clay tablets from around 1800 BCE pose problems giving the sum and the difference of two unknown quantities, then solve them by a fixed rule, half the sum shifted either way by half the difference, in words with no symbols at all.
Solve the system \(y=2x+4\) and \(6x+2y=33\). Nothing requires the pair to be whole. Check the pair in both equations, then enter \(x\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The run is the usual one. Only the ending is not a whole number.

blocks.x: Sometimes the substitution erases the letter entirely. Every \(x\)-term cancels, and a statement with no variable in it is left behind, true or false on its own. 4.3 met this inside one equation. Here the leftover statement is a verdict about the whole system, and the next two problems read one of each kind.
Substitute \(y=4x+5\) into \(8x-2y=6\) and simplify. Every \(x\)-term cancels and a number statement is left. Decide what it means and enter the number of solutions of the system.
hints: 4.3 met a vanishing variable inside one equation. The number statement left behind is the verdict.
\(8x-2(4x+5)\) simplifies to \(-10\), and the equation claims that equals \(6\).
blocks.sol: \(8x-2(4x+5)=8x-8x-10=-10\), so the substituted equation reads \(-10=6\), false at every \(x\), and the system has \(\boxed{0}\) solutions. No pair can make both claims true at once.

blocks.x: When the letter disappears. A false statement means the two claims conflict at every pair, so the system has no solution. That is 5.1's \(m+n=67\) and \(m+n=73\) situation, reached by algebra instead of by staring. A true statement means the second equation repeats the first, so every pair solving one solves both, and the solutions are infinitely many. Substitution is not failing in either case. It is reporting the count.

Substituting \(y=2x+6\) into \(4x-2y=-12\) leaves \(-12=-12\), true for every \(x\). Infinitely many pairs solve the system, but not every pair does. Of \((2,10)\), \((6,18)\), \((10,26)\), \((8,20)\), enter how many solve the system.
hints: Every pair solving the first equation solves both. Pairs off it solve neither.
Test each pair in \(y=2x+6\), first value in for \(x\), second in for \(y\).
blocks.sol: \(10=4+6\), \(18=12+6\), and \(26=20+6\) pass, but \(2(8)+6=22\neq 20\), so \(\boxed{3}\) of the four solve the system. Infinitely many means every pair satisfying the equation, and only those.

blocks.x: Two numbers satisfy \(x-2y=45\) and \(2x+3y=398\). Isolate the coefficient-1 letter, substitute, solve the system, check the pair in both equations, and enter the product \(xy\).
hints: Only \(x\) carries coefficient \(1\). One 4.3 move gives \(x=2y+45\).
Substituting gives \(2(2y+45)+3y=398\), which collects to \(7y+90=398\).

blocks.x: All the systems in this lesson had a letter with coefficient \(1\) or \(-1\), or were already solved for a letter. There is no letter to isolate cleanly in \(9x+7y=76\) and \(5x+8y=72\), so any isolation starts with a division and brings fractions into every later step. Lesson 5.3 introduces elimination, a second method for exactly this case.

review.x: The numbers \(x\) and \(y\) satisfy \(y=x+25\) and \(x+y=71\). Substitute the expression for \(y\) into the second equation, solve, and enter \(x\).
hints: The first equation already gives \(y\) as an expression, so the second equation can be rewritten with only \(x\) in it.
After substituting, the equation reads \(x+(x+25)=71\), so \(2x+25=71\).
review.sol: Substituting gives \(x+(x+25)=71\), so \(2x+25=71\), \(2x=46\), and \(x=\boxed{23}\). Then \(y=48\), and \(23+48=71\) checks.

review.x: The system \(y=2x\) and \(3x+y=40\). The expression for \(y\) has no constant term, and the steps are exactly the same. Substitute, solve, back-substitute, and enter \(y\).
hints: Write \(2x\) in \(y\)'s place in the second equation.
That gives \(3x+2x=40\). Solve for \(x\), then compute \(y\).
review.sol: Substituting gives \(3x+2x=40\), so \(5x=40\) and \(x=8\). Back-substituting, \(y=2(8)=\boxed{16}\). The pair checks in the second equation, since \(24+16=40\).

review.x: The system \(x=y+10\) and \(x+4y=30\) leads with \(x\). Replace the \(x\) of the second equation with \(y+10\), solve for \(y\), back-substitute, and enter \(x\).
hints: Either letter can be the pre-solved one, and the steps do not change.
Substituting gives \((y+10)+4y=30\).

review.x: Solve the system \(y=2x+34\) and \(2x+y=150\). Substitute, solve for \(x\), then finish with a back-substitution and enter \(y\).
hints: Substituting turns the second equation into one with only \(x\), which 4.2 solves.
After substituting, \(2x+(2x+34)=150\), so \(4x+34=150\).

review.x: In \(y=x-5\) and \(3x+2y=50\), the \(y\) slot carries a coefficient, so the substitution needs parentheses. Substitute, distribute, solve the system, and enter \(x+y\).
hints: The \(2\) in \(2y\) multiplies the whole expression that replaces \(y\), not just its first term.
After substituting, the equation reads \(3x+2(x-5)=50\).
review.sol: \(3x+2(x-5)=50\) distributes to \(3x+2x-10=50\), so \(5x=60\) and \(x=12\). Then \(y=12-5=7\) and \(x+y=\boxed{19}\). Check, \(3(12)+2(7)=36+14=50\). Dropping the parentheses would give \(3x+2x-5=50\), which subtracts \(5\) where the equation subtracts \(10\).

review.x: Solve the system \(y=2x+1\) and \(5x+3y=80\). The \(3y\) takes the whole expression as one unit. Substitute with parentheses, distribute, and enter \(y\).
hints: Replacing the \(y\) of \(3y\) must produce \(3(2x+1)\).
Distributing gives \(5x+6x+3=80\).

review.x: Substituting \(y=3x-7\) into \(2x+5y=61\), a student writes \(2x+5\cdot 3x-7\), no parentheses. At every value of \(x\), the student's expression exceeds the faithful \(2x+5(3x-7)\) by the same fixed amount. Enter that amount.
hints: Both expressions carry the same \(x\)-terms, so compare what each one subtracts.
The faithful line subtracts \(35\). The bare line subtracts \(7\).
review.sol: The faithful expression is \(2x+15x-35=17x-35\) and the bare one is \(2x+15x-7=17x-7\), a gap of \(35-7=\boxed{28}\) at every \(x\). The missing parentheses shrink the subtraction from \(35\) to \(7\).

review.x: Neither equation of \(4x+y=231\) and \(2x+3y=233\) is pre-solved. Isolate the coefficient-1 letter with one 4.3 move, substitute into the other equation, and enter \(x\).
hints: Only the \(y\) of the first equation has coefficient \(1\), so isolate it there.
Substituting \(y=231-4x\) gives \(2x+3(231-4x)=233\).

review.x: For \(x+5y=14\) and \(3x+4y=64\), the letter that isolates cleanly is \(x\). Isolate it, substitute into the second equation, solve, and enter \(y\).
hints: \(x\) has coefficient \(1\) in the first equation, so it isolates without dividing.

review.x: Solve \(x=2y+3\) and \(3x+2y=11\). The system leads with \(x\), and the answer is not a whole number. Enter \(y\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Substitute the \(x\)-expression into the second equation, parentheses included.

review.x: In \(4x+y=248\) and \(2x+3y=254\), one letter isolates without fractions and one does not. Pick well, solve the system, and enter the product \(xy\).
hints: Isolating \(x\) from either equation brings in fractions. Isolating the first equation's \(y\) does not.
Substituting \(y=248-4x\) gives \(2x+3(248-4x)=254\).

review.x: Substitute \(y=5x-3\) into \(10x-2y=12\) and simplify. The letter vanishes, and the left side sits the same fixed amount below \(12\) at every \(x\). Enter that amount.
hints: Replace \(y\) with \(5x-3\) in the second equation, then collect the \(x\) terms before deciding anything.
\(10x-2(5x-3)\) simplifies to a constant. Compare it with \(12\).
review.sol: \(10x-2(5x-3)=10x-10x+6=6\), so the substituted equation reads \(6=12\), and the left side sits \(12-6=\boxed{6}\) below the right side at every \(x\). The statement is false everywhere, so the system has no solution.

review.x: Substituting \(y=4x+1\) into \(12x-3y=-3\) leaves \(-3=-3\), a true statement. Every pair solving the first equation solves the system. Of the pairs \((3,13)\), \((0,1)\), \((2,8)\), \((5,20)\), enter how many solve it.
hints: Infinitely many solutions does not mean every pair. Only pairs satisfying the first equation count.
Test each pair in \(y=4x+1\).
review.sol: Testing each pair in \(y=4x+1\), \(13=12+1\) and \(1=0+1\) pass, while \(4(2)+1=9\neq 8\) and \(4(5)+1=21\neq 20\) fail. So \(\boxed{2}\) of the four solve the system.

review.x: For \(x-2y=1\) and \(6x+5y=74\), isolate \(x\), substitute into the second equation, solve the system, and enter \(x+y\).
hints: The subtracted \(2y\) moves to the other side in one addition.

review.x: One number is 5 less than double another, and the two add to 43. In symbols, \(y=2x-5\) and \(x+y=43\). Solve the system and enter the larger number.
hints: The first equation is already solved for \(y\), so substitute \(2x-5\) for \(y\) in the second equation.
review.sol: \(x+(2x-5)=43\) gives \(3x-5=43\), so \(3x=48\) and \(x=16\), then \(y=2(16)-5=27\). The larger number is \(\boxed{27}\). The problem asks for the larger of the two numbers, not for \(x\), so find both values before answering.

review.x: For \(6x+y=37\) and \(4x+3y=90\), isolate the coefficient-1 letter, substitute, and enter \(x\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: \(y\) isolates without dividing, and the fraction only shows up at the very end.
review.sol: \(y=37-6x\), so \(4x+3(37-6x)=90\) gives \(4x+111-18x=90\), then \(111-14x=90\), \(14x=21\), and \(x=\frac{21}{14}=\boxed{\frac{3}{2}}\), with \(y=37-9=28\). The clean isolate keeps fractions out of the middle of the work, not out of the answer.

review.x: In \(3x-y=106\) and \(2x+2y=220\), the \(y\) has coefficient \(-1\), and 4.3's moves still isolate it, \(y=3x-106\). Substitute, solve the system, and enter the product \(xy\).
hints: A coefficient of \(-1\) still isolates in one move, and the expression that results is \(3x-106\).
Substituting gives \(2x+2(3x-106)=220\), which collects to \(8x-212=220\).

blocks.x: Lesson 5.2 closed on a system with no clean isolate, \(9x+7y=76\) and \(5x+8y=72\). Every coefficient is bigger than \(1\), so solving for a letter starts with a division, \(y=\frac{76-9x}{7}\), and fractions appear in every line after that. Set the system aside. It returns as the last problem of this lesson.

At the solution of the system \(4x+7y=50\) and \(3x-7y=13\), each equation's two sides are the same number, so the sum of the left sides equals the sum of the right sides. Write that sum equation, combine like terms on each side, then solve what remains and enter \(x\).
hints: Stack the two equations and add straight down, left side to left side and right side to right side.
The \(+7y\) and \(-7y\) sum to zero, so the sum equation is \(7x=63\).
blocks.sol: Adding the two left sides and the two right sides gives \(7x+0y=63\), so \(7x=63\) and \(x=\boxed{9}\). Back-substituting, \(7y=50-36=14\), so \(y=2\), and \((9,2)\) checks in both originals, \(36+14=50\) and \(27-14=13\). One addition removed \(y\) and left a chapter 4 equation.

blocks.x: Elimination. When the same letter carries opposite coefficients in the two equations, adding the equations term by term makes that letter's terms sum to zero, and one letter remains. Chapter 4 solves the equation that is left, and substituting the value back into either original gives the partner. The addition is legal because at a solution pair both equations are true, so adding the left sides and the right sides adds equal numbers to equal numbers. Every solution of the system satisfies the sum equation too, so no solution is lost.

blocks.x: Solve the system \(7x+3y=9\) and \(2x-3y=18\) by adding the equations, then back-substitute into either original. The ask is \(y\), not \(x\).
hints: The opposite \(y\)-coefficients cancel when the equations are added, but the sum equation has no \(y\) in it, so it cannot answer the ask by itself.
Adding gives \(9x=27\). Find \(x\), then substitute that value into either original equation.
blocks.sol: Adding gives \(9x=27\), so \(x=3\). Then \(21+3y=9\), \(3y=-12\), and \(y=\boxed{-4}\). Elimination finds one letter and back-substitution finds the other, so stopping at \(x=3\) leaves the ask unanswered.

blocks.x: The \(y\)-coefficients of \(7x+2y=62\) and \(3x+2y=30\) are equal, not opposite, so adding gives \(10x+4y=92\) and both letters are still there. Subtract the second equation from the first instead, every term on both sides, back-substitute, and enter \(x+y\).
hints: Subtracting equal numbers from equal numbers is as legal as adding them, and equal coefficients cancel under subtraction.
The left sides subtract term by term, \(7x-3x\) and \(2y-2y\), and the right sides subtract as well.
blocks.sol: Subtracting gives \(4x+0y=32\), so \(x=8\). Then \(56+2y=62\), \(2y=6\), \(y=3\), and \(x+y=\boxed{11}\). The subtraction has to reach the right sides too, \(62-30=32\), not only the columns of letters.

blocks.x: Subtract the whole equation. Subtracting equal numbers from equal numbers also leaves equal results, so one equation can be subtracted from the other, and matching coefficients cancel that way. The minus stands in front of the entire equation being subtracted, so it reaches every one of its terms, signs included, the same rule 4.4 applied to a minus in front of parentheses. The right sides subtract too. The common error is flipping the sign in the matched column and copying the rest, which writes a different equation and lands on a pair that fails the check.

Subtracting \(5x-2y=34\) from \(5x+3y=74\), a student writes \(3y-2y=40\), so \(y=40\), and the check fails. Find the sign the student dropped, redo the subtraction with every term carrying its sign, and enter the correct \(y\).
hints: Subtracting a whole equation subtracts each of its terms, signs included. Look at what the second equation's \(y\)-term actually is.
That term is \(-2y\), so the \(y\)-column is \(3y-(-2y)\), not \(3y-2y\). Redo it, then the right sides.
blocks.sol: The \(y\)-column is \(3y-(-2y)=5y\) and the right sides give \(74-34=40\), so \(5y=40\) and \(y=\boxed{8}\). Subtracting a whole equation puts a minus in front of parentheses, the rule from 4.4, since the left column means \(5x+3y-(5x-2y)\). The student subtracted \(2y\) instead of \(-2y\).

blocks.x: Matched coefficients are luck. When neither equation offers one, 4.2 allows multiplying an equation, both sides, by any nonzero number, and the result is an equivalent equation with the same solutions. So a matching coefficient can be built. Multiply one equation by whatever number its coefficient needs, then add or subtract.
In \(3x+4y=59\) and \(6x+5y=85\), no coefficient matches yet. Multiply the first equation, both sides, by \(2\), then subtract to eliminate \(x\). Solve the system and enter \(x+y\).
hints: Write the doubled first equation out in full, then subtract the second from it column by column, the \(x\) terms, the \(y\) terms, and the right sides.
The doubled first equation is \(6x+8y=118\). Subtract the second equation from that one.
blocks.sol: Doubling the first equation gives \(6x+8y=118\), and subtracting the second leaves \(3y=33\), so \(y=11\). Then \(3x+44=59\) gives \(x=5\), and \(x+y=\boxed{16}\). The scaling has to reach the right side, so the doubled equation ends in \(118\), not \(59\).

blocks.x: Solve \(7x+5y=-1\) and \(3x+15y=-39\). Scale the first equation by \(3\), subtract the second, and enter \(y\). Both right sides are negative, so the subtraction there needs care.
hints: Tripling the first equation makes both \(y\)-columns \(15y\). Scale both sides, so the \(-1\) is tripled as well.
The right sides subtract as \(-3-(-39)\), a difference of two negatives.
blocks.sol: Tripling the first equation gives \(21x+15y=-3\), and subtracting the second leaves \(18x=-3-(-39)=36\), so \(x=2\). Then \(14+5y=-1\) gives \(5y=-15\) and \(y=\boxed{-3}\). The tripled right side is \(-3\), not \(-1\), and subtracting \(-39\) adds \(39\).

blocks.x: Scale both, and pick the cheap letter. When neither coefficient of the chosen letter divides the other, multiply each equation by the number its coefficient needs to reach a common multiple of the two, then add or subtract. Either letter can be eliminated and both choices give the same pair, so the choice is only about the size of the arithmetic. The habit is to eliminate the letter whose two coefficients have the smaller common multiple, which keeps every number in the run small.

In \(6x+7y=56\) and \(3x+5y=31\), one letter eliminates by scaling a single equation, while the other needs both equations scaled to reach \(35\). Pick the cheap one, solve the system, and enter the product \(xy\).
hints: Price the two choices before scaling anything. The \(x\)-coefficients are \(6\) and \(3\), the \(y\)-coefficients are \(7\) and \(5\).
Doubling the second equation makes both \(x\)-columns \(6x\). Subtract, and a \(y\)-equation is left.
blocks.sol: Doubling the second equation gives \(6x+10y=62\), and subtracting the first leaves \(3y=6\), so \(y=2\). Then \(6x+14=56\) gives \(x=7\), and \(xy=\boxed{14}\). Eliminating \(y\) reaches the same pair, but it means scaling to \(35y\) and subtracting \(280-217\) instead of \(62-56\).

blocks.x: Eliminate \(y\) from \(5x+4y=46\) and \(7x-6y=-40\) by scaling both equations so the \(y\)-terms become \(12y\) and \(-12y\). Solve the system, check the pair in both originals, and enter the product \(xy\).
hints: Each equation gets multiplied by whatever its \(y\)-coefficient needs to reach \(12\), and the factor hits both sides, right side included.
The scaled \(y\)-terms are \(12y\) and \(-12y\), which are opposites, so the two equations are added rather than subtracted.
blocks.sol: Three times the first is \(15x+12y=138\), twice the second is \(14x-12y=-80\), and adding them gives \(29x=58\), so \(x=2\). Then \(10+4y=46\) gives \(y=9\), and \(xy=\boxed{18}\). Check \((2,9)\) in both originals, \(10+36=46\) and \(14-54=-40\).

blocks.x: The Chinese Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, compiled roughly two thousand years ago, solves systems of linear equations in its fangcheng chapter by elimination on an array of counting rods, long before the method had a European name.
Solve \(4x+9y=32\) and \(2x+7y=21\) by eliminating \(x\). Every line stays whole until one final division. Enter \(x\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Doubling the second equation matches the \(x\)-columns at \(4x\).
\(y\) comes out whole. Put that \(y\) back into either equation and the coefficient of \(x\) will not divide the right side evenly, which is where the fraction finally shows up.
blocks.sol: Doubling the second equation gives \(4x+14y=42\), and subtracting the first leaves \(5y=10\), so \(y=2\). Then \(2x+14=21\) gives \(2x=7\) and \(x=\boxed{\frac{7}{2}}\). Every line before that division stayed whole, so the only fraction in the problem is the answer itself.

blocks.x: Both letters can cancel at once. When they do, what remains is a statement about numbers alone, true or false on its own. Substitution reached the same situation in 5.2, and the reading is the same here. The leftover statement is a verdict on the whole system, and the next two problems have one of each kind.

Try elimination on \(2x+6y=35\) and \(3x+9y=48\). Scale the first equation by \(3\) and the second by \(2\), then subtract. Both letters cancel and a statement about numbers is left. Decide what it means and enter the number of solutions of the system.
hints: When both letter columns cancel, the number statement left behind is the verdict on the whole system.
Both scalings give the left side \(6x+18y\), while the right sides come out \(105\) and \(96\). Subtract and read what is left.
blocks.sol: The scaled equations are \(6x+18y=105\) and \(6x+18y=96\), and subtracting gives \(0=9\), false at every pair, so the system has \(\boxed{0}\) solutions. That is 5.1's count for conflicting claims, reached here by elimination and in 5.2 by substitution.

blocks.x: When both letters vanish. A false statement like \(0=9\) means the two claims conflict at every pair, so the system has no solution, 5.1's count of zero. A true statement like \(0=0\) means one equation is a scaled copy of the other, so the two make the same claim, every pair solving one solves both, and the solutions are infinitely many. Elimination is not failing in either case. It is reporting the count.

Eliminating on \(3x-5y=12\) and \(6x-10y=24\) leaves \(0=0\), true at every pair, so the system has infinitely many solutions. That does not make every pair a solution. Of \((4,0)\), \((19,9)\), \((14,6)\), \((8,2)\), enter how many solve the system.
hints: \(0=0\) means the second equation is a scaled copy of the first, so a pair solves the system exactly when it solves \(3x-5y=12\).
Substitute each listed pair into \(3x-5y=12\) and count the ones that give \(12\).
blocks.sol: In \(3x-5y\) the four pairs give \(12\), \(12\), \(12\), and \(24-10=14\), so \(\boxed{3}\) of them solve the system. Infinitely many solutions means every pair satisfying the shared equation, not every pair anybody writes down.

blocks.x: Back to the shelved system. In \(9x+7y=76\) and \(5x+8y=72\) no letter isolates without a division, which is what stopped substitution. Elimination isolates nothing, so no division is needed. The \(x\)-coefficients \(9\) and \(5\) both divide \(45\), so scaling the first equation by \(5\) and the second by \(9\) puts \(45x\) in each.
Finish the system 5.2 left unsolved. Scale \(9x+7y=76\) by \(5\) and \(5x+8y=72\) by \(9\), so both carry \(45x\), then subtract and solve. Enter \(y\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Multiplying an equation through by a number keeps the same solution pair, so scaling is safe. The target \(45\) is the smallest number that both \(9\) and \(5\) divide into.
Five times the first equation is \(45x+35y=380\) and nine times the second is \(45x+72y=648\). One subtraction and one division are left.
blocks.sol: The scaled equations are \(45x+35y=380\) and \(45x+72y=648\), and subtracting the first from the second leaves \(37y=268\), so \(y=\boxed{\frac{268}{37}}\), with \(x=\frac{104}{37}\). The work stays in whole numbers until that last division, while isolating a letter in either original equation would start with a division.

blocks.x: Both methods solve every linear system in two variables, so the choice is convenience. An equation already solved for a letter, or a letter with coefficient \(1\) or \(-1\), points to substitution. Coefficients that match, or match after one scaling, point to elimination. Lesson 5.4 takes on systems that need cleanup before either method applies.

review.x: The \(y\)-terms of \(6x+5y=57\) and \(3x-5y=6\) are \(+5y\) and \(-5y\). Add the left sides and add the right sides, solve the one-letter equation that remains, and enter \(x\).
hints: Opposite coefficients sum to zero, so the equation left after adding carries only one letter.
The left sides add to \(9x\) and the right sides add to \(63\).
review.sol: Adding gives \(9x=63\), so \(x=\boxed{7}\), and \(5y=57-42=15\) gives \(y=3\). Check in the second equation, \(21-15=6\).

review.x: Solve \(6x+y=40\) and \(3x-y=14\) by adding the two equations, then back-substituting into either original. Enter \(y\).
hints: Write the two equations one above the other and add left side to left side, right side to right side. Watch what \(+y\) and \(-y\) contribute to that sum.
The sum is \(9x=54\). That gives \(x\), and the ask is \(y\), so put the \(x\) into either original equation.
review.sol: Adding gives \(9x=54\), so \(x=6\), and \(6(6)+y=40\) gives \(y=\boxed{4}\). Check in the second equation, \(3(6)-4=14\). Adding removes one letter and back-substitution finds the other.

review.x: The \(x\)-terms of \(-4x+9y=42\) and \(4x+11y=78\) are already opposites, so adding removes \(x\) and leaves an equation in \(y\). Solve the system and enter \(x\).
hints: Line the two equations up and add them column by column. The \(x\)-column disappears and the \(y\)-terms combine into \(9y+11y\).
The sum is \(20y=120\). Solve it for \(y\), then put that value into either original equation to get \(x\).
review.sol: Adding the equations gives \(20y=120\), so \(y=6\). The first equation becomes \(-4x+54=42\), so \(-4x=-12\) and \(x=\boxed{3}\). The second equation checks, \(4(3)+11(6)=12+66=78\).

review.x: Two numbers add to \(94\) and differ by \(22\). Write the two facts as a system, add the equations to eliminate a letter, and enter the smaller number.
hints: With \(x\) the larger number and \(y\) the smaller, the facts are \(x+y=94\) and \(x-y=22\), and the \(y\)-terms are opposites.
Adding gives \(2x=116\). The ask is the other number.
review.sol: The system is \(x+y=94\) and \(x-y=22\). Adding gives \(2x=116\), so \(x=58\), and \(58+y=94\) gives \(y=\boxed{36}\). Check, \(58-36=22\). A sum fact and a difference fact always add straight to a one-letter equation.

review.x: The \(y\)-coefficients of \(9x+5y=120\) and \(4x+5y=70\) are both \(5\), equal rather than opposite, so adding keeps both letters. Subtract the second equation from the first instead, every term on both sides, and enter \(x\).
hints: Equal coefficients cancel under subtraction the way opposite ones cancel under addition.
The left sides subtract to \(5x\), and the right sides subtract too, \(120-70\).
review.sol: Subtracting the second equation from the first gives \(5x=50\), so \(x=\boxed{10}\). Then \(5y=70-40=30\) gives \(y=6\), and the first equation checks, \(90+30=120\). Subtracting the other way gives \(-5x=-50\) and the same \(x\).

review.x: Subtract \(2x-3y=-11\) from \(2x+6y=52\). The \(x\)-column cancels. Finish the solve and enter \(x\).
hints: The minus applies to every term of the equation being subtracted, so both the \(-3y\) and the \(-11\) change sign.
The \(y\)-column is \(6y-(-3y)\) and the right side is \(52-(-11)\). Solve that for \(y\), then back-substitute for \(x\).
review.sol: Subtracting gives \(9y=63\), so \(y=7\), and \(2x+42=52\) gives \(2x=10\) and \(x=\boxed{5}\). The pair checks in \(2x-3y=-11\), since \(10-21=-11\). Both the \(-3y\) and the \(-11\) flipped sign when that equation was subtracted.

review.x: Both \(7x+5y=81\) and \(7x-3y=-15\) lead with \(7x\). Subtract the second equation from the first, flipping the sign of every term of the subtracted equation, the right side included. Enter \(y\).
hints: The subtracted equation is negative in two places, the \(y\)-term and the right side, and both need the same care.
\(5y-(-3y)=8y\). Work out \(81-(-15)\) the same way.
review.sol: Subtracting term by term, \(5y-(-3y)=8y\) and \(81-(-15)=96\), so \(8y=96\) and \(y=\boxed{12}\). Back-substituting gives \(x=3\), and \(7(3)-3(12)=21-36=-15\) checks the second equation. Writing \(5y-3y\) instead of \(5y+3y\) is the usual slip.

review.x: In \(8x+5y=73\) and \(4x+15y=99\), scaling the first equation once makes the \(y\)-coefficients match. Make that match, eliminate \(y\), and enter \(x\).
hints: The \(y\)-coefficients are \(5\) and \(15\), and \(5\) reaches \(15\) in a single scaling.
Multiply every term of the first equation by \(3\), the right side included, then subtract the second equation.
review.sol: Three times the first equation is \(24x+15y=219\), and subtracting the second gives \(20x=120\), so \(x=\boxed{6}\). Then \(48+5y=73\) gives \(y=5\), and \(4(6)+15(5)=99\) checks. Scaling has to reach the right side too.

review.x: Solve \(5x+9y=87\) and \(10x+7y=86\). Doubling the first equation, both sides, lines up the \(x\)-terms at \(10x\). Enter \(y\).
hints: Doubling means every term, the \(9y\) and the \(87\) as well, not only the \(5x\).
Twice the first equation is \(10x+18y=174\). Subtract the second from it.
review.sol: Twice the first equation is \(10x+18y=174\). Subtracting the second gives \(11y=88\), so \(y=\boxed{8}\), with \(x=3\) from \(5x+72=87\). Check in the second equation, \(30+56=86\).

review.x: No coefficients in \(9x+y=43\) and \(5x+3y=19\) match yet, but one scaling of the first equation, both sides, brings the \(y\)-columns together. Solve the system and enter \(y\).
hints: The \(y\)-coefficients are \(1\) and \(3\), so tripling the first equation matches them.
Three times the first equation is \(27x+3y=129\). Subtract the second, then back-substitute.
review.sol: Three times the first equation is \(27x+3y=129\). Subtracting the second gives \(22x=110\), so \(x=5\), and \(45+y=43\) gives \(y=\boxed{-2}\). Check in the second equation, \(25-6=19\).

review.x: For \(3x+7y=41\) and \(12x+9y=69\), the \(x\)-coefficients first meet at \(12\) and the \(y\)-coefficients first meet at \(63\). Enter the letter that is cheaper to eliminate.
hints: Cheaper means less multiplying. For each target, count how many of the two equations you would have to scale up before those terms match.
The second equation already carries \(12x\), so only the first has to be scaled to reach it. Neither equation carries \(63y\).
review.sol: Matching at \(12x\) takes one scaling, the first equation times \(4\), while matching at \(63y\) takes two, the first times \(9\) and the second times \(7\), so the cheaper letter is \(\boxed{x}\). Both routes end at the same pair \((2,5)\), and the only difference is how large the numbers get.

review.x: Solve \(6x+7y=75\) and \(4x+5y=51\). Neither \(x\)-coefficient divides the other, so scale both equations to eliminate \(x\). Enter the product \(xy\).
hints: \(6\) and \(4\) both reach \(12\), one by doubling and one by tripling.
The scaled equations are \(12x+14y=150\) and \(12x+15y=153\). Subtract.
review.sol: Twice the first is \(12x+14y=150\) and three times the second is \(12x+15y=153\). Subtracting gives \(y=3\), and \(6x+21=75\) gives \(6x=54\) and \(x=9\), so \(xy=\boxed{27}\). Check in the second equation, \(36+15=51\).

review.x: The \(x\)-coefficients of \(2x+3y=16\) and \(7x+5y=23\) are \(2\) and \(7\), whose only common factor is \(1\). Scale both equations to a common \(x\)-coefficient, subtract, and enter \(x\).
hints: Neither coefficient is a multiple of the other, so both equations have to scale. The smallest common multiple of \(2\) and \(7\) is \(14\).
Seven times the first is \(14x+21y=112\) and twice the second is \(14x+10y=46\). Subtract.
review.sol: Seven times the first is \(14x+21y=112\) and twice the second is \(14x+10y=46\). Subtracting gives \(11y=66\), so \(y=6\), and \(2x+18=16\) gives \(2x=-2\) and \(x=\boxed{-1}\). Check in the second equation, \(-7+30=23\). A solution pair can have a negative member.

review.x: Solve \(7x+9y=29\) and \(6x+3y=17\). Nothing here is fractional until the last step. Enter \(y\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: One \(y\)-coefficient is a multiple of the other, so scaling a single equation lines the two \(y\)-terms up. Subtracting then removes \(y\).
Three times the second equation is \(18x+9y=51\). Subtract \(7x+9y=29\) from it.
review.sol: Three times the second equation is \(18x+9y=51\), and subtracting the first gives \(11x=22\), so \(x=2\). Then \(6(2)+3y=17\) gives \(3y=5\) and \(y=\boxed{\frac{5}{3}}\). Check in the first equation, \(7(2)+9\cdot\frac{5}{3}=14+15=29\).

review.x: Eliminate a letter from \(3x+8y=44\) and \(6x+16y=77\). Both letters cancel at once and a number statement is left. Read it and enter the number of solutions of the system.
hints: When both letters cancel, the statement left behind is the verdict on the whole system.
Doubling the first equation gives \(6x+16y=88\), while the second says that same left side is \(77\).
review.sol: Twice the first equation is \(6x+16y=88\). Subtracting the second gives \(0=11\), false at every pair, so the system has \(\boxed{0}\) solutions. The same left side cannot be \(88\) and \(77\) at once, so the two equations contradict each other and no pair passes both.

review.x: Elimination on \(5x-2y=15\) and \(15x-6y=45\) leaves \(0=0\), true everywhere, so the system has infinitely many solutions. That does not make every pair one of them. Of \((3,0)\), \((5,5)\), \((6,7)\), \((4,1)\), enter how many solve the system.
hints: \(0=0\) means the second equation is a scaled copy of the first, so a pair solves the system exactly when it solves \(5x-2y=15\).
Substitute each of the four pairs into \(5x-2y=15\) and count the ones that come out to \(15\).
review.sol: The left sides are \(15-0=15\), \(25-10=15\), \(30-14=16\), and \(20-2=18\), so \(\boxed{2}\) of the four solve the system. Infinitely many solutions means every pair satisfying the shared equation, and only those.

review.x: For exactly one value of \(k\), elimination on \(8x+12y=372\) and \(2x+3y=k\) leaves \(0=0\) and the system has infinitely many solutions. Every other value of \(k\) leaves a false statement instead. Enter \(k\).
hints: Infinitely many solutions means one equation is a scaled copy of the other, right side included.
The first left side is \(4\) times the second, so the right sides have to stand in that same ratio.
review.sol: Since \(8x+12y\) is \(4\) times \(2x+3y\), the two claims agree at every pair exactly when \(372=4k\), so \(k=\boxed{93}\). Check, multiplying \(2x+3y=93\) by \(4\) gives \(8x+12y=372\). Any other value makes one left side equal two different numbers, and the count drops to zero.

review.x: Solve \(10x+6y=162\) and \(7x+9y=147\). One letter's coefficients meet at \(18\) and the other's meet at \(70\). Eliminate the cheaper one, scaling both equations, and enter the product \(xy\).
hints: The cheaper meeting point is \(18\), so aim to make both \(y\) terms into \(18y\). Ask what each equation has to be multiplied by to land there.
Multiply the first equation by \(3\) and the second by \(2\). Both then carry \(18y\), so one subtraction clears \(y\) and leaves an equation in \(x\) alone.
review.sol: Three times the first is \(30x+18y=486\) and twice the second is \(14x+18y=294\). Subtracting gives \(16x=192\), so \(x=12\), and \(120+6y=162\) gives \(6y=42\) and \(y=7\), so \(xy=\boxed{84}\). Check in the second equation, \(84+63=147\). Eliminating \(x\) instead would push the scaled equations past \(1000\).

blocks.x: The choice between substitution and elimination comes down to coefficients, and a coefficient is only readable once an equation is written \(ax+by=c\). Plenty of systems are not written that way. Every system in this lesson is an ordinary one after a cleanup move from 4.4, and the new fact is that each of the two equations is cleaned on its own.

Eliminating \(y\) from \(6(x-2y)+7y=29\) and \(4x+9y=155\) means comparing the two coefficients of \(y\). In the second equation that coefficient is \(9\). Enter the coefficient of \(y\) in the first equation, once its left side is written as \(ax+by\).
hints: To eliminate \(y\) you compare the two coefficients of \(y\), and that coefficient is whatever multiplies \(y\) once the left side is collected into one \(x\)-term and one \(y\)-term.
Distribute the \(6\) over \(x-2y\) to get \(6x-12y\), then combine that with the \(+7y\) outside the parentheses.
blocks.sol: Distributing gives \(6x-12y+7y\), and \(-12y+7y=-5y\), so the left side is \(6x-5y\) and the coefficient of \(y\) is \(\boxed{-5}\). The printed \(7\) is not the coefficient on its own, since distributing the \(6\) produces a second \(y\)-term, \(-12y\), that combines with it.

blocks.x: Distributing and combining like terms turns \(6(x-2y)+7y=29\) into \(6x-5y=29\), so the system is \(6x-5y=29\) and \(4x+9y=155\). Eliminate \(x\) the 5.3 way, back-substitute, and enter \(x\).
hints: Nothing about elimination changes now that both equations are in \(ax+by=c\) form. Compare the two coefficients on \(x\) before scaling anything.
The \(x\)-coefficients \(6\) and \(4\) both divide \(12\), so double the first equation and triple the second.
blocks.sol: Doubling the first equation gives \(12x-10y=58\) and tripling the second gives \(12x+27y=465\). Subtracting the first of those from the second leaves \(37y=407\), so \(y=11\), and then \(6x-55=29\) gives \(6x=84\) and \(x=\boxed{14}\). Check, \(6(14)-5(11)=84-55=29\) and \(4(14)+9(11)=56+99=155\). Only the cleanup was new. Once both equations are in \(ax+by=c\) form, elimination is the same work as in 5.3.

blocks.x: Clean each side first. Distributing, from 2.1, and combining like terms, from 2.4, rewrite one side of an equation as an equal expression, so the new equation is true for exactly the same pairs as the old one, and the other equation of the system is untouched. A coefficient is the number multiplying a letter once that collecting is done, so the \(7\) printed in \(6(x-2y)+7y\) is not the coefficient of \(y\). Until both letter terms are collected there is nothing to compare and no letter to isolate.

Neither equation of \(4(x+3y)-5y=123\) and \(6x-3(y-4)=75\) is in \(ax+by=c\) form yet. Clean each one, solve the system, and enter the product \(xy\). In the second equation the factor in front of the parentheses is \(-3\), and it reaches both terms inside, signs included.
hints: Expand and combine on the left of each equation the 2.1 way before a solving method is picked. The constant that comes out of the second expansion belongs on the right side with the \(75\).
\(-3(y-4)\) is \(-3y+12\), not \(-3y-12\), so the second equation cleans to \(6x-3y=63\) and then \(2x-y=21\). Isolating \(y\) there costs one move.
blocks.sol: Distributing gives \(4x+12y-5y=123\), so \(4x+7y=123\), and \(6x-3y+12=75\), so \(6x-3y=63\) and \(2x-y=21\). Then \(y=2x-21\), and \(4x+7(2x-21)=123\) gives \(18x=270\), \(x=15\), \(y=9\), and \(xy=\boxed{135}\). The \(-3\) reaches the \(-4\) as well, which is why the constant lands as \(+12\).

blocks.x: Neither \(9x-33=3y+132\) nor \(4y+5x=2x+20\) reads \(ax+by=c\), since one has a number on the left and each has letter terms on both sides. Use 4.3's balance moves on each, then solve the cleaned system and enter \(y\).
hints: Take one equation at a time. Move every letter term to the left side and every number to the right side, doing the same thing to both sides at each step.
The first equation collects to \(9x-3y=165\), and dividing both sides by \(3\) gives \(3x-y=55\). The second collects to \(3x+4y=20\), so the \(x\)-columns match.
blocks.sol: Collecting the first equation gives \(9x-3y=165\), and dividing both sides by \(3\) gives \(3x-y=55\). The second collects to \(3x+4y=20\). Subtracting the cleaned first equation from the cleaned second leaves \(5y=-35\), so \(y=\boxed{-7}\), with \(3x=55-7=48\) and \(x=16\). Check \((16,-7)\) in both originals, \(144-33=111=-21+132\) and \(-28+80=52=32+20\). Once both equations read \(ax+by=c\), one subtraction finished the system.

blocks.x: Standard form is \(ax+by=c\). Both letter terms on the left, the number alone on the right. 4.3's balance moves put any linear equation into that form by adding or subtracting the same thing on both sides. Two equations in that form can be stacked so the \(x\)-terms share a column and the \(y\)-terms share another, which is what 5.3 subtracts, and a coefficient of \(1\) is easy to spot, which is what 5.2 isolates without dividing. Both equations have to be in that form before there is anything to compare.
Clean \(7x+4y=2x+3y+86\) and \(4(x+2y)-x-3y=144\) into \(ax+by=c\) form. Exactly one of the two letters can then be isolated with no division at all. Enter the value of that letter.
hints: Nothing can be compared until both equations are in \(ax+by=c\) form. Combine like terms in the first, and distribute the \(4\) in the second.
The cleaned system is \(5x+y=86\) and \(3x+5y=144\). Scan its four coefficients for a \(1\).
blocks.sol: Combining like terms in the first equation gives \(5x+y=86\), and distributing in the second gives \(4x+8y-x-3y=144\), so \(3x+5y=144\). The only coefficient of \(1\) is on the \(y\) of the first equation, so \(y=86-5x\), and \(3x+5(86-5x)=144\) becomes \(430-22x=144\), so \(22x=286\) and \(x=13\). Then \(y=86-65=\boxed{21}\). Eliminating \(y\) means scaling one equation to \(5y\), and eliminating \(x\) means scaling both to \(15x\), so \(y\) is the cheap letter either way.

blocks.x: 4.4 cleared a fractional equation by multiplying both sides by a common denominator of its fractions, and one well-chosen multiplication removed every fraction at once. A system has two equations to run that on. The next two problems put fractions in one equation, then in both.
Solve \(\frac{x}{3}+\frac{y}{2}=17\) and \(4x-3y=60\). Only one of the two equations has fractions in it, and the other already reads \(ax+by=c\). Enter \(x\).
hints: The second equation has no fractions in it, so it needs no multiplier at all. Leave it as it is and work on the first.
The denominators \(3\) and \(2\) both divide \(6\). Multiply every term of the first equation by \(6\), the \(17\) included.
blocks.sol: Multiplying the first equation by \(6\) gives \(2x+3y=102\), and adding \(4x-3y=60\) leaves \(6x=162\), so \(x=\boxed{27}\), with \(3y=102-54=48\) and \(y=16\). Check, \(9+8=17\) and \(108-48=60\). Each equation is cleaned on its own, so only the fractional one is multiplied.

blocks.x: Solve \(\frac{x}{10}+\frac{y}{3}=15\) and \(\frac{x}{9}+\frac{y}{2}=19\). Each equation has its own pair of denominators, so clear the fractions one equation at a time. Enter \(x\).
hints: Clearing the first equation takes a multiple of \(10\) and \(3\). Clearing the second takes a multiple of \(9\) and \(2\). Choose the two multipliers separately.
Multiply the first equation by \(30\) and the second by \(18\), every term on both sides.
blocks.sol: Multiplying the first equation by \(30\) gives \(3x+10y=450\), and multiplying the second by \(18\) gives \(2x+9y=342\). Doubling the first result gives \(6x+20y=900\), tripling the second gives \(6x+27y=1026\), and subtracting leaves \(7y=126\), so \(y=18\). Then \(3x+180=450\) gives \(3x=270\) and \(x=\boxed{90}\). The multiplier for each equation is built from that equation's own denominators, so the two multipliers are different.
