blocks.cap: The multiplier for a row comes from the denominators in that row and nothing else, so \(24\) clears the first and \(35\) clears the second. Each multiplier reaches every term on both sides of its own row, and neither one clears the other row.

blocks.x: Each equation gets its own multiplier. The multiplier for an equation is a common denominator of the fractions in that equation, and every term on both sides of that equation is multiplied by it. Nothing about the other equation affects that choice, so the two multipliers are usually different numbers, \(30\) for one and \(18\) for the other. In 4.4 there was a single equation to clear, so one multiplier was the whole job. A system has two, and each is cleared on its own.

A student clears \(\frac{x}{3}+4=\frac{y}{9}\) by multiplying by \(9\) and gets \(3x+4=y\). Paired with \(5x+y=124\) that line gives \((15,49)\), and the check fails, since \(\frac{15}{3}+4=9\) while \(\frac{49}{9}\) is not \(9\). Redo the clearing and enter the correct \(y\).
hints: Multiplying by \(9\) has to multiply every term, and the first equation has three terms, not two.
The \(+4\) sits on the same side as \(\frac{x}{3}\), so it gets multiplied as well and becomes \(36\).
blocks.sol: Multiplying every term by \(9\) gives \(3x+36=y\). Substituting into \(5x+y=124\) gives \(5x+3x+36=124\), so \(8x=88\), \(x=11\), and \(y=3(11)+36=\boxed{69}\). Check, \(\frac{11}{3}+4=\frac{23}{3}\) and \(\frac{69}{9}=\frac{23}{3}\). Every term means the \(+4\) as well, so \(3x+4=y\) is a different equation, and the pair it gives fails the original.

blocks.x: A decimal coefficient is a count of tenths or hundredths, so a decimal equation is really a fraction equation, and one multiplication clears it just as before. The power of ten still comes from one equation at a time, so the two multipliers need not match.
Solve \(0.6x+0.4y=37\) and \(0.07x-0.05y=1.9\). The power of ten that clears an equation comes from the finest decimal place in that equation. Enter \(x\).
hints: The first equation has nothing finer than tenths, and the second has hundredths, so the two powers of ten are not the same.
Multiply the first equation by \(10\) and the second by \(100\), both sides each time. The right sides then read \(370\) and \(190\).
blocks.sol: Clearing gives \(6x+4y=370\) and \(7x-5y=190\). Scaling to \(20y\) and \(-20y\) gives \(30x+20y=1850\) and \(28x-20y=760\), and adding leaves \(58x=2610\), so \(x=\boxed{45}\), with \(y=25\). Check, \(27+10=37\) and \(3.15-1.25=1.9\). Multiplying the second equation by \(10\) would leave \(0.7x\) and \(0.5y\) behind.

blocks.x: In 1585 the Flemish engineer Simon Stevin published De Thiende, a pamphlet of a few pages that introduced decimal fractions to Europe and argued that every fraction should be written in tenths.

One shape from 4.4 is worth naming again. A fraction bar is a grouping symbol, so a numerator with two terms is grouped as a whole and needs parentheses the moment it is multiplied. Inside a system that numerator carries two letters instead of one, and that is the only difference from 4.4.
Solve \(\frac{4x-y}{5}=\frac{x+2y}{4}\) and \(x+y=125\). Each side of the first equation is a single fraction and nothing else, so two multiplications clear it. Enter \(x\).
hints: This is 4.4's shape with two letters in each numerator instead of one. The fraction bar groups its whole numerator.
Multiplying by \(4\) and then by \(5\) leaves \(4(4x-y)=5(x+2y)\). Collect that into \(ax+by=c\) before using \(x+y=125\).
blocks.sol: Multiplying by \(4\) and then by \(5\) gives \(4(4x-y)=5(x+2y)\), so \(16x-4y=5x+10y\) and \(11x=14y\). With \(x=125-y\), \(11(125-y)=14y\) gives \(25y=1375\), \(y=55\), and \(x=\boxed{70}\). Check, \(70+55=125\), and both sides of the first equation come out \(45\), from \(\frac{225}{5}\) and \(\frac{180}{4}\). In \(ax+by=c\) form the cleaned equation is \(11x-14y=0\), so \(c\) is allowed to be \(0\).

blocks.x: Cross-multiplying is still two multiplications. From \(\frac{p}{q}=\frac{r}{s}\), multiplying both sides by \(q\) and then by \(s\) gives \(ps=qr\), which is 4.4's rule with two letters in each numerator instead of one. It applies only when each side is a single fraction and nothing else. With an extra term on either side, clear the equation by a common multiplier instead. Cleaning this shape often leaves \(0\) on the right, which is an ordinary \(ax+by=c\) with \(c=0\).

Some systems are not linear in \(x\) and \(y\) at all. In \(\frac{9}{x}+\frac{2}{y}=41\) the letters are in the denominators, and multiplying through by \(xy\) produces an \(xy\) term rather than a linear equation. Both equations are linear in \(\frac{1}{x}\) and \(\frac{1}{y}\) though, and those two pieces can be given names.
In \(\frac{4}{x}+\frac{3}{y}=44\) and \(\frac{7}{x}-\frac{3}{y}=11\), set \(u=\frac{1}{x}\) and \(v=\frac{1}{y}\). Solve the system in \(u\) and \(v\) and enter \(u\).
hints: Rewrite every \(\frac{1}{x}\) as \(u\) and every \(\frac{1}{y}\) as \(v\), so \(\frac{4}{x}\) is \(4u\) and \(\frac{3}{y}\) is \(3v\).
The renamed system is \(4u+3v=44\) and \(7u-3v=11\), an ordinary 5.3 problem with opposite \(v\)-coefficients.
blocks.sol: In \(u\) and \(v\) the system is \(4u+3v=44\) and \(7u-3v=11\). The \(v\)-coefficients are opposites, so adding gives \(11u=55\) and \(u=\boxed{5}\). Then \(20+3v=44\) gives \(v=8\), and since \(u=\frac{1}{x}\) and \(v=\frac{1}{y}\), the original values are \(x=\frac{1}{5}\) and \(y=\frac{1}{8}\).

blocks.x: Name the repeated piece, then convert back. When both equations are linear in the same two pieces, giving those pieces names makes an ordinary system for 5.2 or 5.3. Here the pieces are \(\frac{1}{x}\) and \(\frac{1}{y}\), and elsewhere they are \(\sqrt{x}\) and \(\sqrt{y}\), or \(x^2\) and \(y^2\). Converting back undoes the naming, so \(u=\frac{1}{x}\) gives \(x=\frac{1}{u}\), and stopping at \(u\) reports a different quantity, since \(u=5\) means \(x=\frac{1}{5}\). A letter in a denominator cannot be \(0\), so the conversion back always works.

Solve \(\frac{14}{x}+\frac{6}{y}=5\) and \(\frac{21}{x}-\frac{4}{y}=1\). Neither equation has the form \(ax+by=c\), but naming the two repeated pieces yourself turns both into that form. Solve the renamed system and enter \(x\) itself, not the value of the new letter.
hints: Neither equation is linear in \(x\) and \(y\), but both are linear in \(\frac{1}{x}\) and \(\frac{1}{y}\). Name those two pieces.
With \(u=\frac{1}{x}\) and \(v=\frac{1}{y}\) the system is \(14u+6v=5\) and \(21u-4v=1\). Solve that by elimination, then convert with \(x=\frac{1}{u}\).
blocks.sol: With \(u=\frac{1}{x}\) and \(v=\frac{1}{y}\) the system is \(14u+6v=5\) and \(21u-4v=1\). Doubling the first and tripling the second gives \(28u+12v=10\) and \(63u-12v=3\), and adding leaves \(91u=13\), so \(u=\frac{1}{7}\) and \(v=\frac{1}{2}\). Then \(x=\frac{1}{u}=\boxed{7}\), with \(y=2\). Check in the originals, \(\frac{14}{7}+\frac{6}{2}=5\) and \(\frac{21}{7}-\frac{4}{2}=1\).

blocks.x: Every system in this lesson was one cleanup move away from an ordinary system, and the choice between substitution and elimination came after that move rather than before it. 5.5 starts further back. The equations are not written down at all, only English sentences, and building the system is the work.

review.x: The first equation of the system \(3(x+2y)=54\) and \(x-y=6\) is not in \(ax+by=c\) form yet. Rewrite it, solve the system, and enter \(x\).
hints: Divide the first equation by \(3\), or distribute it, so both equations read \(ax+by=c\).
The cleaned pair is \(x+2y=18\) and \(x-y=6\), and the \(x\)-columns already match, so subtracting cancels them.
review.sol: Dividing the first equation by \(3\) gives \(x+2y=18\). Subtracting \(x-y=6\) leaves \(3y=12\), so \(y=4\). Back-substituting into \(x-y=6\) gives \(x=\boxed{10}\). Check, \(3(10+8)=54\) and \(10-4=6\). Distributing to \(3x+6y=54\) and then dividing by \(3\) lands on the same equation, so either route cleans it.

review.x: The system is \(8x-4(y-3)=52\) and \(2x+y=34\). Clean the first equation into \(ax+by=c\) form, then solve the system. The ask is \(y\), not \(x\).
hints: Multiply both terms inside the parentheses by \(-4\), the \(-3\) included. Two negatives give a positive, so that second term comes out positive rather than negative.
The cleaned first equation is \(2x-y=10\), whose \(y\)-term is the opposite of the \(+y\) in the second, so add the two equations.
review.sol: Distributing gives \(8x-4y+12=52\), so \(8x-4y=40\) and \(2x-y=10\). Adding \(2x+y=34\) leaves \(4x=44\), so \(x=11\) and \(y=\boxed{12}\). Check \((11,12)\) in the original first equation, \(88-4(9)=52\). The product of \(-4\) and \(-3\) is \(+12\), and dropping that sign change is the usual slip here.

review.x: Both sides of \(9x-y=5x+3y+44\) carry letters. Put that equation into \(ax+by=c\) form, solve the system it makes with \(2x+5y=120\), and enter \(x\).
hints: Letters on both sides. Move them all to the left with 4.3's moves before doing anything else.
Collecting the letters gives \(4x-4y=44\), and dividing by \(4\) leaves \(x-y=11\), where \(x\) has coefficient \(1\).
review.sol: Collecting the letters on the left gives \(4x-4y=44\), and dividing by \(4\) leaves \(x-y=11\), so \(x=y+11\). Then \(2(y+11)+5y=120\) collects to \(7y=98\), so \(y=14\) and \(x=\boxed{25}\). Check, \(9(25)-14=211\) and \(5(25)+3(14)+44=211\). In \(x-y=11\) the letter \(x\) has coefficient \(1\), so isolating it brings in no fractions.

review.x: The equation \(12+3x=5y-8\) is not in \(ax+by=c\) form. Rewrite it in that form, solve it together with \(2x+3y=69\), and enter the value of \(y\).
hints: Get the first equation into \(ax+by=c\) form before anything else. Move both variable terms to the left side and the constant to the right side.
The cleaned first equation is \(3x-5y=-20\). Multiply it by \(2\) and multiply \(2x+3y=69\) by \(3\) to line up \(6x\) in both.
review.sol: Subtract \(12\) from both sides and \(5y\) from both sides to get \(3x-5y=-20\). Multiply that by \(2\) for \(6x-10y=-40\), multiply \(2x+3y=69\) by \(3\) for \(6x+9y=207\), and subtract the first of those from the second for \(19y=247\), so \(y=\boxed{13}\). Then \(3x=45\) and \(x=15\). In the original, \(12+45=57\) and \(65-8=57\).

review.x: Solve \(\frac{x}{4}+\frac{y}{5}=14\) and \(3x-2y=36\). Only one of the two equations has fractions to clear. Enter \(x\).
hints: Only \(\frac{x}{4}+\frac{y}{5}=14\) has denominators. Find one multiplier that clears both the \(4\) and the \(5\), and leave \(3x-2y=36\) as it stands.
Multiplying through by \(20\) gives \(5x+4y=280\), right side included. From there the \(y\)-terms are \(4y\) and \(-2y\), one doubling apart.
review.sol: Multiplying the first equation by \(20\) gives \(5x+4y=280\). Doubling \(3x-2y=36\) gives \(6x-4y=72\), and adding leaves \(11x=352\), so \(x=\boxed{32}\). Back-substituting gives \(y=30\). Check, \(\frac{32}{4}+\frac{30}{5}=8+6=14\) and \(96-60=36\). Only the equation with denominators needs a multiplier, and it has to reach the right side, which is why the \(14\) becomes \(280\).

review.x: Solve \(\frac{x+2y}{3}-\frac{y}{4}=9\) and \(2x-y=26\). Multiply the first equation by the least common denominator to clear the fractions, then solve the cleaned system. Enter \(x\).
hints: A fraction bar acts like parentheses around everything above it, so the whole of \(x+2y\) is one quantity in that first equation.
Multiply every term of the first equation by \(12\). That gives \(4(x+2y)-3y=108\), which still needs distributing.
review.sol: Multiplying the first equation by \(12\) gives \(4(x+2y)-3y=108\), so \(4x+5y=108\). The second equation gives \(y=2x-26\), so \(4x+10x-130=108\) and \(14x=238\), so \(x=\boxed{17}\). Then \(y=8\). Check in the first equation, \(\frac{17+16}{3}-\frac{8}{4}=11-2=9\). Multiply the whole numerator and not just the \(x\), which is why \(x+2y\) stays in parentheses until the distributing step.

review.x: Solve \(\frac{x}{2}+\frac{y}{7}=13\) and \(\frac{x}{8}+\frac{y}{5}=9\). The denominators differ from one equation to the other, so clear each equation with its own multiplier. Enter \(x\).
hints: The denominators of the first equation are \(2\) and \(7\), and the denominators of the second are \(8\) and \(5\). Multiply an equation by the least common multiple of its own two denominators.
Multiplying the first equation by \(14\) and the second by \(40\) clears every fraction, as long as the right sides \(13\) and \(9\) are multiplied as well.
review.sol: Multiplying the first equation by \(14\) gives \(7x+2y=182\), and the second by \(40\) gives \(5x+8y=360\). Four times the first is \(28x+8y=728\), and subtracting \(5x+8y=360\) leaves \(23x=368\), so \(x=\boxed{16}\). Then \(y=35\). Check, \(\frac{16}{8}+\frac{35}{5}=9\). The smallest multiplier for each equation comes from its own denominators.

review.x: Solve \(0.8x+0.5y=18\) and \(0.2x-0.3y=6.2\). Clear the decimals from each equation first, then eliminate. Enter \(y\).
hints: The finest decimal place in each equation is tenths, so multiplying by \(10\) makes every number in both equations whole.
Multiplying both equations by \(10\) gives \(8x+5y=180\) and \(2x-3y=62\), since the \(6.2\) is multiplied as well.
review.sol: Multiplying each equation by \(10\) gives \(8x+5y=180\) and \(2x-3y=62\). Four times the second is \(8x-12y=248\), and subtracting that from the first leaves \(17y=-68\), so \(y=\boxed{-4}\). Back-substitution gives \(x=25\). Check, \(0.8(25)+0.5(-4)=20-2=18\) and \(0.2(25)-0.3(-4)=5+1.2=6.2\).

review.x: Solve \(0.7x+0.4y=45\) and \(0.03x+0.08y=3.5\). Clear the decimals in each equation first, then solve. Enter \(x\).
hints: The first equation stops at tenths and the second at hundredths, so ask what power of ten each one needs.
Multiply the first equation by \(10\) and the second by \(100\). The right sides scale too, so the \(3.5\) becomes \(350\).
review.sol: Multiplying the first equation by \(10\) gives \(7x+4y=450\), and the second by \(100\) gives \(3x+8y=350\). Doubling \(7x+4y=450\) gives \(14x+8y=900\), and subtracting \(3x+8y=350\) leaves \(11x=550\), so \(x=\boxed{50}\). Then \(y=25\). Check in the second equation, \(0.03(50)+0.08(25)=3.5\). A multiplier of \(10\) there would leave \(0.3x\), since a hundredths place needs a multiplier of \(100\).

review.x: The system is \(0.25x+0.4y=17\) and \(x-y=3\). A student clears the first equation by multiplying by \(100\) and writes \(25x+40y=17\), leaving the right side alone. That line has no whole-number solution with \(x-y=3\) at all, which is the first sign something is wrong. Redo the clearing and enter the correct \(x\).
hints: Multiplying an equation by \(100\) multiplies both sides, so the \(17\) changes too.
Since \(17\times 100=1700\), the cleared equation is \(25x+40y=1700\), and every term in it is a multiple of \(5\).
review.sol: Multiplying every term by \(100\) gives \(25x+40y=1700\), and dividing by \(5\) gives \(5x+8y=340\). With \(x=y+3\), \(5(y+3)+8y=340\) gives \(13y=325\), so \(y=25\) and \(x=\boxed{28}\). Check, \(0.25(28)+0.4(25)=7+10=17\) and \(28-25=3\). Multiplying only the left side changes the equation, since \(25x+40y=17\) is the same as \(0.25x+0.4y=0.17\).

review.x: The system is \(\frac{x}{2}-6=\frac{y}{8}\) and \(2x+y=138\). A student multiplies the first equation by \(8\), writes \(4x-6=y\), and reports \(x=24\). Testing \((24,90)\) in the first equation gives \(6\) on the left and \(11.25\) on the right. Enter the correct value of \(x\).
hints: Multiplying by \(8\) applies to every term on the left side, not only \(\frac{x}{2}\).
Clear the first equation correctly, then add it to \(2x+y=138\) to eliminate \(y\).
review.sol: Multiplying every term by \(8\) gives \(4x-48=y\), so \(4x-y=48\). Adding \(2x+y=138\) gives \(6x=186\), so \(x=\boxed{31}\). The student multiplied only the two fraction terms and left the \(-6\) unchanged. With \(y=76\), the check is \(15.5-6=9.5\) and \(\frac{76}{8}=9.5\).

review.x: Solve \(\frac{2x+y}{4}=\frac{x+5y}{6}\) and \(x+y=99\). Clean the first equation into \(ax+by=c\) before using the second. Enter \(y\).
hints: Each side of the first equation is a single fraction and nothing else, so multiplying both sides by \(4\) and then by \(6\) clears both denominators.
Clearing gives \(6(2x+y)=4(x+5y)\). Distribute both sides, then move every \(x\)-term and \(y\)-term to one side to reach \(ax+by=c\).
review.sol: Multiplying both sides by \(4\) and then by \(6\) gives \(6(2x+y)=4(x+5y)\), so \(12x+6y=4x+20y\) and the cleaned form is \(8x-14y=0\), or \(4x=7y\). With \(x=99-y\), \(4(99-y)=7y\) gives \(396-4y=7y\), so \(11y=396\) and \(y=\boxed{36}\). Then \(x=63\), and the original equation checks, \(\frac{162}{4}=\frac{243}{6}=40.5\). The fraction bar groups the whole numerator, so each numerator needs parentheses once the denominators are gone.

review.x: Solve \(\frac{x-y}{4}=\frac{y}{6}+3\) and \(x+y=52\). The right side of the first equation is a fraction plus a whole number rather than a single fraction, so clear it with one multiplier instead of cross-multiplying. Enter \(x\).
hints: The right side is a fraction plus \(3\), not a single fraction, so cross-multiplying the equation as written is not valid.
Multiply every term of the first equation by \(12\), the \(3\) on the right included.
review.sol: Multiplying the first equation by \(12\) gives \(3(x-y)=2y+36\), so \(3x-5y=36\). With \(x=52-y\), \(3(52-y)-5y=36\) gives \(156-8y=36\), so \(8y=120\), \(y=15\), and \(x=\boxed{37}\). Check, \(\frac{37-15}{4}=\frac{11}{2}\) and \(\frac{15}{6}+3=\frac{11}{2}\). One multiplication by \(12\) clears both denominators, and the \(3\) on the right is a term to multiply like any other.

review.x: Clean \(3(x+2y)-2y=71\) and \(8x+9y=2x+2y+131\) into \(ax+by=c\) form. One letter's two coefficients meet at a smaller least common multiple than the other letter's, so eliminating it takes less scaling. Enter that letter.
hints: Neither equation is in \(ax+by=c\) form yet, so distribute the \(3\) in the first and move \(2x\) and \(2y\) to the left in the second.
The cleaned system is \(3x+4y=71\) and \(6x+7y=131\). Compare the least common multiple of \(3\) and \(6\) with the least common multiple of \(4\) and \(7\).
review.sol: Distributing gives \(3x+6y-2y=71\), so \(3x+4y=71\), and collecting the second gives \(6x+7y=131\). The \(x\)-coefficients \(3\) and \(6\) meet at \(6\), which takes one scaling, while the \(y\)-coefficients \(4\) and \(7\) meet at \(28\), which takes two, so the cheaper letter is \(\boxed{x}\). Both routes reach the same pair \((9,11)\), and the only difference is how large the numbers get.

review.x: In \(\frac{1}{x}+\frac{5}{y}=33\) and \(\frac{3}{x}-\frac{1}{y}=19\), set \(u=\frac{1}{x}\) and \(v=\frac{1}{y}\). Solve the renamed system and enter \(u\).
hints: Every \(\frac{1}{x}\) becomes \(u\) and every \(\frac{1}{y}\) becomes \(v\), so \(\frac{5}{y}\) is \(5v\).
The renamed system is \(u+5v=33\) and \(3u-v=19\). Solving the second for \(v\) takes no division, so substitution finishes it.
review.sol: Renaming gives \(u+5v=33\) and \(3u-v=19\). Solving the second for \(v\) gives \(v=3u-19\), so \(u+5(3u-19)=33\), which is \(16u-95=33\), then \(16u=128\) and \(u=\boxed{8}\). Then \(v=5\), and the check gives \(8+25=33\) and \(24-5=19\). Since \(u=\frac{1}{x}\) and \(v=\frac{1}{y}\), the original solution is \(x=\frac{1}{8}\) and \(y=\frac{1}{5}\).

review.x: Solve the system \(\frac{2}{x}+\frac{3}{y}=30\) and \(\frac{5}{x}-\frac{2}{y}=37\). Enter \(x\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Neither equation is linear in \(x\) and \(y\), but both are linear in \(\frac{1}{x}\) and \(\frac{1}{y}\). Name those two pieces first.
With \(u=\frac{1}{x}\) and \(v=\frac{1}{y}\) the system reads \(2u+3v=30\) and \(5u-2v=37\). Eliminate \(v\), then remember the ask is \(x=\frac{1}{u}\), not \(u\).
review.sol: With \(u=\frac{1}{x}\) and \(v=\frac{1}{y}\) the system is \(2u+3v=30\) and \(5u-2v=37\). Doubling the first gives \(4u+6v=60\) and tripling the second gives \(15u-6v=111\), and the sum is \(19u=171\), so \(u=9\) and \(v=4\). Then \(y=\frac{1}{4}\) and \(x=\frac{1}{u}=\boxed{\frac{1}{9}}\). The ask is \(x\), not \(u\), so \(9\) is one step short of the answer.

review.x: Solve \(\frac{x+y}{2}+\frac{y}{3}=23\) and \(0.15x-0.2y=1.5\). Clear each equation to the form \(ax+by=c\) first. Enter the product \(xy\).
hints: The denominators in the first equation are \(2\) and \(3\), and the second equation runs to hundredths, so choose a separate multiplier for each equation.
Multiplying by \(6\) and by \(100\) gives \(3x+5y=138\) and \(15x-20y=150\), and dividing that second one by \(5\) gives \(3x-4y=30\). Both have \(3x\).
review.sol: Multiplying the first equation by \(6\) gives \(3(x+y)+2y=138\), so \(3x+5y=138\). Multiplying the second by \(100\) gives \(15x-20y=150\), and dividing by \(5\) gives \(3x-4y=30\). Subtracting leaves \(9y=108\), so \(y=12\), and \(3x=138-60=78\), so \(x=26\) and \(xy=\boxed{312}\). Check, \(\frac{38}{2}+4=23\) and \(3.9-2.4=1.5\). Clearing fractions and clearing decimals are the same move, one multiplier taken from the denominators and one from a power of ten.

review.x: Nonnegative numbers \(a\) and \(b\) satisfy \(\sqrt{a}+3\sqrt{b}=41\) and \(\sqrt{a}-\sqrt{b}=13\). Neither equation is linear in \(a\) and \(b\), but both are linear in \(\sqrt{a}\) and \(\sqrt{b}\). Name those two pieces, solve, convert back, and enter \(a\).
hints: Set \(u=\sqrt{a}\) and \(v=\sqrt{b}\). The system becomes \(u+3v=41\) and \(u-v=13\), which 5.3 handles.
Subtracting the second equation from the first gives \(4v=28\). Once \(u\) is known, \(a=u^2\), not \(u\).
review.sol: With \(u=\sqrt{a}\) and \(v=\sqrt{b}\) the system is \(u+3v=41\) and \(u-v=13\). Subtracting gives \(4v=28\), so \(v=7\) and \(u=20\). Then \(a=u^2=\boxed{400}\). Squaring is what converts back, so \(b=49\), and the check gives \(20+21=41\) and \(20-7=13\). Entering \(20\) reports \(\sqrt{a}\) rather than \(a\).

review.x: Positive numbers \(m\) and \(n\) satisfy \(m^2+n^2=289\) and \(m^2-n^2=161\). The system is linear in \(m^2\) and \(n^2\), so name those two pieces. Enter \(m+n\).
hints: Set \(u=m^2\) and \(v=n^2\). The system reads \(u+v=289\) and \(u-v=161\), a sum-and-difference pair.
Adding gives \(2u=450\). Converting back takes a square root of each, and the ask is \(m+n\), not \(u+v\).
review.sol: With \(u=m^2\) and \(v=n^2\) the system is \(u+v=289\) and \(u-v=161\). Adding gives \(2u=450\), so \(u=225\) and \(v=64\). Both numbers are positive, so \(m=15\) and \(n=8\), and \(m+n=\boxed{23}\). The naming is what makes the system linear, since \(m^2\) and \(n^2\) appear only as whole pieces.

blocks.x: Here the equations are yours to write. A story states its facts in plain English, and the two letters, what each one stands for, and one equation for each fact all have to be written down first. After that the system is an ordinary one and 5.2 or 5.3 finishes it. Try the next two stories before any of this has a name.

A ferry charges one fixed fare for a motorcycle and another for a car. The fares from 4 motorcycles and 3 cars come to 64 dollars, and the fares from 6 motorcycles and 7 cars come to 126 dollars. Enter the fare for one motorcycle, in dollars.
hints: Two fares are unknown here, one for a motorcycle and one for a car. Name both, then write one equation for each of the two totals.

With \(m\) dollars for a motorcycle and \(c\) dollars for a car, \(4m+3c=64\) and \(6m+7c=126\). No letter has coefficient \(1\), so isolating one brings fractions. Scale both equations and eliminate the 5.3 way instead.
blocks.sol: With \(m\) dollars for a motorcycle and \(c\) for a car, \(4m+3c=64\) and \(6m+7c=126\). Tripling the first and doubling the second gives \(12m+9c=192\) and \(12m+14c=252\), and subtracting leaves \(5c=60\), so \(c=12\), then \(4m=64-36=28\) and \(m=\boxed{7}\). Check, \(6(7)+7(12)=42+84=126\). Neither total is made of one fare alone, so no single total gives a fare by itself, and the story needs two letters.

blocks.x: A photo lab made 143 prints on Tuesday, some small and some large. The number of small prints was 5 more than twice the number of large prints. Enter how many large prints the lab made that day.
hints: Name both counts before anything else, \(L\) for the large prints and \(S\) for the small prints. Two separate facts are stated here, the total of 143 and the description of \(S\) in terms of \(L\), so two equations come out of them.
With \(L\) large prints and \(S\) small prints the total is \(L+S=143\). Twice the large count is \(2L\), so the second sentence reads \(S=2L+5\). Replace \(S\) in the total.
blocks.sol: \(L+S=143\) and \(S=2L+5\), so \(L+(2L+5)=143\), \(3L=138\), and \(L=\boxed{46}\), with \(S=97\). Check, \(2(46)+5=97\) and \(46+97=143\). Five more than twice \(L\) is \(2L+5\) and not \(2(L+5)\), since only the large count is doubled.

blocks.x: The two-variable routine. This is 4.5's routine with the count raised from one letter to two. Say what both letters stand for, units included. Translate each separate fact into its own equation, one equation per fact. Solve with 5.2 or 5.3, build the quantity the question names, then check the pair against the story. What is new is naming a second quantity, finding a second fact, and reading the closing sentence again at the end, since with two numbers in hand the one asked for is often neither of them.
A greenhouse bench holds shallow trays of 12 cells and deep trays of 20 cells, 37 trays and 588 cells in all. Enter how many of the trays are deep.
hints: Name the two tray counts. The bench is counted twice, once in trays and once in cells, so there are two facts to translate.
With \(s\) shallow trays and \(d\) deep trays, \(s+d=37\) and \(12s+20d=588\). Substitute \(s=37-d\).
blocks.sol: \(12(37-d)+20d=588\), so \(444+8d=588\), then \(8d=144\) and \(d=\boxed{18}\). The other 19 trays are shallow, and \(12(19)+20(18)=588\). Counting trays and counting cells are separate measurements, so the story needs two equations, not one.

blocks.x: A school stationery order was 52 items, all pens and markers. Pens cost 3 dollars each, markers cost 7 dollars each, and the whole order cost 264 dollars. Enter how many of the items were pens.
hints: Write one equation for the 52 items and a second for the 264 dollars.
With \(p\) pens and \(m\) markers, \(p+m=52\) and \(3p+7m=264\). Rewrite the first as \(p=52-m\) and put that into the second.
blocks.sol: With \(p\) pens and \(m\) markers, \(p+m=52\) and \(3p+7m=264\). Put \(p=52-m\) into the cost equation to get \(156+4m=264\), so \(4m=108\) and \(m=27\). Then \(p=52-27=\boxed{25}\). The count and the cost are two separate facts about the same order, so each one gets its own equation.

blocks.x: One separate fact, one equation. A fact is separate when it can be checked on its own. Counting the trays and counting the cells are two different measurements of the same bench, so \(s+d=37\) and \(12s+20d=588\) are two claims rather than one claim written twice. That is the test to run on a story before writing anything down. Translate the same fact twice, once in each of its two wordings, and the second equation is only a scaled copy of the first. Eliminating then gives \(0=0\), which is 5.3's case of infinitely many pairs.
A hardware bin holds 118 fasteners, each one a bolt or a screw. The number of bolts is 14 less than three times the number of screws. Enter how many bolts are in the bin.
hints: Name both counts, \(s\) for the screws and \(b\) for the bolts. The total of 118 is one fact and the sentence comparing the two counts is the other.
Three times the screw count is \(3s\), and 14 less than that is \(3s-14\), so \(b=3s-14\). Put that into \(s+b=118\).
blocks.sol: With \(s\) screws and \(b\) bolts, \(s+b=118\) and \(b=3s-14\). Substituting gives \(s+(3s-14)=118\), so \(4s=132\) and \(s=33\), which makes \(b=3(33)-14=\boxed{85}\). Check, \(33+85=118\). Fourteen less than \(3s\) is \(3s-14\) and not \(14-3s\), and the reversed version gives a negative bolt count.

blocks.x: Solving a system produces two numbers, and the question often asks for a third, the difference between them, the larger of the two, or a cost built from both. The work is the same either way. What changes is which number gets typed, and stopping at a letter's value is the most common way to work a story correctly and still answer it wrong.

A campsite charges one price per tent night and one price per cabin night, unchanged all season. Three tent nights and two cabin nights cost 214 dollars. Five tent nights and four cabin nights cost 396 dollars. Enter how much more one cabin night costs than one tent night, in dollars.
hints: Name the two nightly prices and write one equation for each booking. Neither equation has a letter with coefficient 1, so elimination is the cheaper route.

With \(t\) and \(c\) in dollars per night, \(3t+2c=214\) and \(5t+4c=396\). Doubling the first equation matches the \(c\)-columns at \(4c\). The closing sentence asks for a difference, not for either nightly price.
blocks.sol: Doubling \(3t+2c=214\) gives \(6t+4c=428\), and subtracting \(5t+4c=396\) leaves \(t=32\). Then \(96+2c=214\) gives \(c=59\), and the ask is \(c-t=59-32=\boxed{27}\). Check, \(5(32)+4(59)=396\). Typing \(59\) answers a question the problem did not ask, since \(59\) is the cabin price and the story asked for the gap between the two prices.

blocks.x: Answer the question that was asked. The two letters are yours to name and the question was fixed before you named them, so there is no reason the answer has to be one of them. Once the pair is found, read the closing sentence again and build the quantity it names, \(c-t\), the larger of the two, the cost of one of each. A pair found correctly and typed as the wrong quantity is marked exactly like a pair found wrong.

A bakery sold 141 loaves, sourdough and rye, with 27 fewer rye loaves than sourdough. Let \(s\) be the number of sourdough loaves and \(r\) the number of rye loaves. A student writes \(s+r=141\) and \(s=r-27\), solves that pair correctly, and both of the student's equations check against the pair that comes out. Fix the equation that is a wrong translation and enter the correct number of rye loaves.
hints: The student's arithmetic is sound, so the error is in the translation. Solve the student's pair, then read the result against the sentence about 27 fewer rye loaves than sourdough.
84 rye against 57 sourdough makes rye the larger count, so the minus sits on the wrong letter. The story says \(r=s-27\).
blocks.sol: The story makes rye the smaller count, so \(r=s-27\). Then \(s+(s-27)=141\), giving \(2s=168\) and \(s=84\), so \(r=\boxed{57}\). The wrong pair and the right pair are the same two numbers swapped, and no algebraic check tells them apart. Only the English says which count is the larger one.

blocks.x: Check the pair against the story. Substituting a solution into the equations you wrote always works, so that check cannot catch a bad translation. Read the two numbers back into the story's sentences one at a time instead. With two letters there is a second way to go wrong, which of the two quantities each letter stands for, and the pair \((57,84)\) satisfies \(s=r-27\) exactly while the English says rye is the smaller count. Only the story rejects it.

A boat moving with a current covers ground at its own still-water speed plus the current's speed, and moving against it at its own speed minus the current's speed. Both speeds are unknown, so name them \(b\) and \(c\). Each trip is one fact, so a round trip is a two-fact story.

blocks.cap: Moving with the current the boat covers ground at \(b+c\), and moving against it at \(b-c\). Two trips on the same river state two facts about the same two letters, which is a system.

blocks.x: A river tour boat runs 90 km downstream in 3 hours, then the same 90 km back upstream in 5 hours. The current holds one steady speed all day, and the boat's speed in still water is the same on both legs. Enter that still-water speed, in km per hour.
hints: Each leg has an actual speed you can work out right away, distance divided by time. That is \(90\div 3\) one way and \(90\div 5\) the other.

Call the boat's still-water speed \(b\) and the current's speed \(c\). The current is with the boat downstream and against it upstream, so \(b+c=30\) and \(b-c=18\), and the \(c\)-terms are already opposite.
blocks.sol: Let \(b\) be the boat's speed in still water and \(c\) the current's speed. Each leg's actual speed is distance over time, \(90\div 3=30\) downstream and \(90\div 5=18\) upstream, so \(b+c=30\) and \(b-c=18\). Adding gives \(2b=48\), so \(b=\boxed{24}\), with \(c=6\). The current is with the boat one way and against it the other, so the two \(c\)-terms are opposite and one addition finishes the system.

blocks.x: A small plane covers 1400 km with a steady wind in 4 hours, then covers the same 1400 km back against that wind in 5 hours. The wind holds one steady speed and the plane's speed in still air is the same on both legs. Enter the wind's speed, in km per hour.
hints: Two speeds are unknown here, the plane's speed in still air and the wind's speed, so give each one a letter. With the wind those two speeds add, and against the wind they subtract.
Each leg gives a ground speed, \(1400\div 4=350\) with the wind and \(1400\div 5=280\) against it, so \(p+w=350\) and \(p-w=280\). Subtracting the second equation from the first removes \(p\).
blocks.sol: The ground speeds are \(1400\div 4=350\) and \(1400\div 5=280\), so \(p+w=350\) and \(p-w=280\). Subtracting the second equation from the first gives \(2w=70\), so \(w=\boxed{35}\), with \(p=315\). Check, \(1400\div 350=4\) and \(1400\div 280=5\). The ask is the wind's speed, so \(315\) is not the value to enter.

blocks.x: Around 800 CE Alcuin of York, a scholar at Charlemagne's court, compiled Propositiones ad Acuendos Juvenes, Problems to Sharpen the Young, fifty-three puzzles told as short stories about ferrymen, granaries and flocks.

Counts are not the only facts a story can state. A measured length is a fact too, and it translates the same way. Prealgebra 11.5 gives a rectangle's perimeter as \(2L+2W\), so a stated perimeter is one equation, and any second length measured across the same rectangle is the other. Two measurements pin down both dimensions.
A rectangular garden bed is edged with 100 m of timber all the way around. A soaker hose runs along one full length and both widths, and it measures 64 m. Enter the length of the bed, in meters.
hints: Name the length \(L\) and the width \(W\), both in meters, and write one equation for the timber and one for the hose. The timber goes all the way around, so it uses each dimension twice.
The system is \(2L+2W=100\) and \(L+2W=64\). Both equations carry \(2W\), so subtracting one from the other clears \(W\) in a single move.
blocks.sol: The timber gives \(2L+2W=100\) and the hose gives \(L+2W=64\). Both carry \(2W\), so subtracting the second from the first leaves \(L=\boxed{36}\). Then \(36+2W=64\) gives \(W=14\). Check, \(2(36)+2(14)=100\) and \(36+28=64\). Each measured length in the story is its own equation, and two of them are enough to give both dimensions.

blocks.x: A two-digit number is not the sum of its digits and not their product. With tens digit \(t\) and units digit \(u\) the number is worth \(10t+u\), since a digit in the tens place is worth ten times its face value. Reversing the two digits gives \(10u+t\). Both are ordinary expressions in two letters, so a fact about either one is an equation.
The digits of a two-digit number add to 11, and reversing the digits gives a number 27 greater than the original. Enter the original number.
hints: The two letters are the digits, not the number. Write the original as \(10t+u\) and the reversed number as \(10u+t\).
\((10u+t)-(10t+u)\) collects to \(9u-9t\), so the second fact is \(u-t=3\). Pair that with \(t+u=11\).
blocks.sol: The reversal fact is \((10u+t)-(10t+u)=27\), which collects to \(9u-9t=27\), so \(u-t=3\). With \(t+u=11\), adding gives \(2u=14\), so \(u=7\) and \(t=4\), and the number is \(\boxed{47}\). Solving gives the two digits, and the number still has to be rebuilt as \(10t+u\). Typing \(4\) or \(7\) answers a question the story did not ask.

blocks.x: Naming the right two quantities is most of the work. Write both meanings down with units before anything else, the number of deep trays, the current's speed in kilometers per hour, the tens digit. Name the wrong two and the system is still solvable, the arithmetic is still clean, and the pair at the end answers a different question. No later step can undo that. The choice is free, so pick the two quantities the story's facts are about, since each fact can then be translated word for word.

A repair counter charges one fixed price to reseal a window and one to rehang a door. One week it resealed 12 windows and rehung 7 doors for 438 dollars. The next week it resealed 9 windows and rehung 11 doors for 432 dollars. Enter the total cost of one reseal and one rehang, in dollars.
hints: The counts of jobs are given, so the two unknowns are the price of a reseal and the price of a rehang. Name those two prices and write one equation for each week's takings.
The system is \(12w+7d=438\) and \(9w+11d=432\). Neither letter has coefficient \(1\), so eliminate one by scaling. The reseal coefficients \(12\) and \(9\) both divide \(36\).
blocks.sol: With \(w\) the price of a reseal and \(d\) the price of a rehang, the two facts are \(12w+7d=438\) and \(9w+11d=432\). Scaling the first by \(3\) and the second by \(4\) gives \(36w+21d=1314\) and \(36w+44d=1728\), and subtracting leaves \(23d=414\), so \(d=18\). Then \(12w+126=438\) gives \(w=26\), so \(w+d=\boxed{44}\). Neither price on its own is the answer, since the question asks for the sum.

blocks.x: Every story here named two quantities and stated two facts, and each system was written one sentence at a time. Some stories name three, a triangle's three angles or three prices on one receipt. Three quantities, three facts. Lesson 5.6, Three or More Variables, raises the count, and elimination still applies, clearing one letter at a time.

review.x: A bike shop charges one fixed price to true a wheel and one fixed price to replace a brake pad. Two wheel truings and three pad replacements cost 61 dollars, and two truings and one pad replacement cost 39 dollars. Enter the price of one wheel truing, in dollars.
hints: Every truing costs the same and every pad replacement costs the same, so name those two prices and write one equation for each visit.
With \(t\) the truing price and \(p\) the pad price, \(2t+3p=61\) and \(2t+p=39\). Both visits hold two truings, so subtracting one equation from the other removes \(t\).
review.sol: With \(t\) the price of one truing and \(p\) the price of one pad replacement, \(2t+3p=61\) and \(2t+p=39\). Subtracting the second from the first leaves \(2p=22\), so \(p=11\), and then \(2t+11=39\) gives \(2t=28\) and \(t=\boxed{14}\). Both visits hold the same two truings, so the 22 dollar gap is the cost of two pad replacements.

review.x: A jar holds 45 marbles, each one red or blue. Each red marble weighs 6 grams, each blue marble weighs 4 grams, and the marbles weigh 232 grams in all. Enter how many of the marbles are red.
hints: Name the two counts first. Count the marbles for one equation, then weigh them for the other.
With \(r\) red marbles and \(b\) blue, \(r+b=45\) and \(6r+4b=232\). Put \(45-r\) in for \(b\) in the weight equation.
review.sol: With \(r\) red marbles and \(b\) blue, \(r+b=45\) and \(6r+4b=232\). Put \(45-r\) in for \(b\) to get \(6r+4(45-r)=232\), so \(2r+180=232\) and \(r=\boxed{26}\). The other 19 marbles are blue, and \(26\cdot 6+19\cdot 4=232\) grams.

review.x: A vending machine holds 30 bars, all of them granola bars or protein bars. Granola bars sell for 2 dollars each and protein bars sell for 3 dollars each, and the 30 bars are worth 79 dollars in all. Enter how many of the bars are protein bars.
hints: The 30 bars and the 79 dollars are two separate facts about the machine, so write one equation for each.
With \(g\) granola bars and \(p\) protein bars, \(g+p=30\) and \(2g+3p=79\). Substitute \(g=30-p\) into the second equation.
review.sol: With \(g\) granola bars and \(p\) protein bars, \(g+p=30\) and \(2g+3p=79\). Substitute \(g=30-p\) into the second equation. Then \(2(30-p)+3p=79\), so \(60+p=79\) and \(p=\boxed{19}\). The other 11 bars are granola, and \(2\cdot 11+3\cdot 19=79\).

review.x: A workshop packs hinges into small crates and large crates, each crate size holding a fixed number of hinges. One shipment of 4 small crates and 3 large crates holds 117 hinges. Another shipment of 2 small crates and 5 large crates holds 139 hinges. Enter how many hinges one large crate holds.
hints: Two numbers are unknown, the hinges in a small crate and the hinges in a large crate. Each shipment is one equation about that same pair.
With \(x\) hinges in a small crate and \(y\) in a large one, \(4x+3y=117\) and \(2x+5y=139\). Double the second equation and the \(x\) terms match.
review.sol: Let \(x\) be the hinges in a small crate and \(y\) the hinges in a large crate. The first shipment gives \(4x+3y=117\) and the second gives \(2x+5y=139\). Doubling the second gives \(4x+10y=278\), and subtracting the first leaves \(7y=161\), so \(y=\boxed{23}\). A small crate holds \(12\) hinges, and \(4(12)+3(23)=117\) matches the first shipment.

review.x: A print shop charges the same price for every poster and the same price for every sticker. One order of 4 posters and 3 stickers cost 41 dollars. Another order of 2 posters and 7 stickers cost 37 dollars. Enter the price of one poster, in dollars.
hints: Each order mixes both items, so one order alone leaves both prices open. Let \(p\) be the dollar price of one poster and \(s\) the dollar price of one sticker, and write what each order says.
The two orders read \(4p+3s=41\) and \(2p+7s=37\). Doubling the second makes its poster term \(4p\), matching the first.
review.sol: With \(p\) dollars for a poster and \(s\) dollars for a sticker, the two orders read \(4p+3s=41\) and \(2p+7s=37\). Doubling the second gives \(4p+14s=74\), and subtracting the first leaves \(11s=33\), so \(s=3\) and \(4p=41-9=32\), which makes \(p=\boxed{8}\). The prices fit the story, 4 posters and 3 stickers cost \(32+9=41\) dollars and 2 posters and 7 stickers cost \(16+21=37\) dollars.

review.x: Every crate of apples weighs the same and every crate of pears weighs the same. Three crates of apples and two crates of pears weigh 63 kg together, and one crate of apples weighs 6 kg more than one crate of pears. Enter the weight of one crate of pears, in kilograms.
hints: Use one letter for the weight of one crate of apples and another for the weight of one crate of pears, both in kilograms. The 58 is a total, not one of the two letters.
With \(a\) and \(p\) for those two weights, the facts are \(3a+2p=63\) and \(a=p+6\). Put \(p+6\) in for \(a\) in the first equation.
review.sol: Let \(a\) be the weight of one crate of apples in kilograms and \(p\) the weight of one crate of pears. Then \(3a+2p=63\) and \(a=p+6\), so \(3(p+6)+2p=63\), giving \(5p+18=63\) and \(p=\boxed{9}\). Check, \(a=15\) and \(3(15)+2(9)=63\). The 3 and the 2 are crate counts and the letters are weights, so \(3a\) is the weight of all three apple crates.

review.x: A nursery's fern count is 8 less than three times its palm count, and the two counts add to 140. Enter how many palms the nursery has.
hints: Name the palm count \(p\) and the fern count \(f\), then write one equation for the comparison and one for the total of \(140\).
Eight less than three times \(p\) is \(3p-8\), so \(f=3p-8\). Substitute that into \(f+p=140\).
review.sol: With \(p\) palms and \(f\) ferns, \(f=3p-8\) and \(f+p=140\), so \((3p-8)+p=140\), giving \(4p=148\) and \(p=\boxed{37}\). Check, \(f=103\), \(103+37=140\) and \(3(37)-8=103\). Reversing the order to \(f=8-3p\) gives \(p=-66\), a negative palm count, so the order the sentence names is what the translation has to keep.

review.x: A stall sold 56 cups of cider. Small cups cost 3 dollars each and large cups cost 5 dollars each, and the stall took in 204 dollars from those 56 cups. Enter how many more small cups than large cups it sold.
hints: Name the two counts, then write one fact about the number of cups and one about the number of dollars. Solve for both counts first, then read the closing sentence again.
With \(s\) small cups and \(L\) large, the cup count gives \(s+L=56\). For the money, each small cup is worth 3 dollars and each large one is worth 5.
review.sol: With \(s\) small cups and \(L\) large, \(s+L=56\) and \(3s+5L=204\). Substituting \(s=56-L\) gives \(3(56-L)+5L=204\), so \(168+2L=204\), \(L=18\), and \(s=38\). The ask is \(s-L=38-18=\boxed{20}\). The question asks for the difference, not for either count, so the subtraction at the end is easy to skip.

review.x: A ranger counted deer and elk on one range. Three times the deer count is 40 more than the elk count, and the elk count is 8 less than twice the deer count. Enter how many elk the ranger counted.
hints: Neither sentence gives a total, so both facts are comparisons. Name the deer count \(d\) and the elk count \(e\), then translate one sentence each.
The first sentence reads \(3d=e+40\) and the second reads \(e=2d-8\). Substituting the second into the first leaves one letter.
review.sol: With \(d\) deer and \(e\) elk, \(3d=e+40\) and \(e=2d-8\). Substituting gives \(3d=(2d-8)+40\), so \(d=32\), and then \(e=2(32)-8=\boxed{56}\). Check, \(3(32)=96\) and \(56+40=96\). A story can pin a pair down with two comparisons and no total at all.

review.x: An airport walkway is 96 m long. Walking along it in the direction it moves, a traveler covers the 96 m in 24 seconds. Walking back along it against its direction, at the same walking speed, the traveler covers the same 96 m in 48 seconds. Enter that walking speed in meters per second, the speed the traveler would walk on a floor that does not move.
hints: The traveler's own walking speed and the walkway's speed are the two unknowns, and each trip covers the same 96 m at a different ground speed.
Each trip gives a ground speed, \(96\div 24\) one way and \(96\div 48\) the other. Along the walkway that ground speed is \(w+m\), and against it \(w-m\).
review.sol: The two ground speeds are \(96\div 24=4\) and \(96\div 48=2\). With \(w\) the walking speed and \(m\) the walkway's speed, \(w+m=4\) and \(w-m=2\). Adding the two gives \(2w=6\), so \(w=\boxed{3}\). Then \(m=1\), which fits both times. With only one trip you would know just \(w+m\), so the second trip is what separates the two speeds.

review.x: A rectangular courtyard has a perimeter of 84 m, and its length is 4 m more than its width. Enter its area, in square meters.
hints: Let \(L\) be the length in meters and \(W\) the width in meters. The perimeter of a rectangle is \(2L+2W\), so one equation is \(2L+2W=84\).
Dividing both sides of \(2L+2W=84\) by \(2\) gives \(L+W=42\). The second equation comes from the length being 4 more than the width, and the answer is the product of the two sides, not either one.
review.sol: With \(L\) the length and \(W\) the width, \(2L+2W=84\) and \(L=W+4\). Dividing the first by \(2\) gives \(L+W=42\), and substituting \(L=W+4\) gives \(2W+4=42\), so \(W=19\) and \(L=23\). The area is \(23\times 19=\boxed{437}\) square meters. Neither letter is the answer on its own, since the question asks for the product of the two sides.

review.x: Plum boxes sell for 4 dollars and fig boxes sell for 7 dollars. A stall sold 11 more plum boxes than fig boxes and took in 187 dollars from those boxes. Let \(p\) be the number of plum boxes and \(f\) the number of fig boxes. Nia writes \(f=p+11\) and \(4p+7f=187\), solves that pair correctly, and gets \(p=10\) and \(f=21\). Her values satisfy both equations she wrote. Fix the wrong translation and enter the correct number of fig boxes.
hints: Nia's arithmetic is sound, so the mistake is in one of the two equations. Read her pair against the sentence about 11 more plum boxes than fig boxes.
Her pair has 10 plum boxes and 21 fig boxes, so figs come out larger. In the story plums are the larger count, so the first equation should read \(p=f+11\).
review.sol: The stall sold 11 more plum boxes than fig boxes, so the first equation should read \(p=f+11\). Then \(4(f+11)+7f=187\) gives \(11f+44=187\), so \(11f=143\) and \(f=\boxed{13}\). Then \(p=24\), and \(4(24)+7(13)=96+91=187\). Nia's two values are whole numbers and they fit both of the equations she wrote, so only a reread of the English sentence catches the error.

review.x: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 95 cm, and each of its two equal sides is 5 cm shorter than twice the base. Enter the length of the base, in centimeters.
hints: Two lengths are unknown, the base and one of the two equal sides. Name them \(b\) and \(s\), both in centimeters, and remember the perimeter counts the equal side twice.
The perimeter gives \(2s+b=95\), and 5 less than twice the base is \(2b-5\), so \(s=2b-5\). Substitute that into the perimeter equation.
review.sol: With \(b\) the base and \(s\) one equal side, \(2s+b=95\) and \(s=2b-5\). Substituting gives \(2(2b-5)+b=95\), so \(5b-10=95\) and \(b=\boxed{21}\). Check against the story, \(s=2(21)-5=37\) and \(2(37)+21=95\). The perimeter counts the equal side twice, so the first equation is \(2s+b\) and not \(s+b\).

review.x: A two-digit number is 7 times the sum of its digits, and reversing its digits gives a number 18 less than the original. Enter the original number.
hints: The letters are the digits, not the number. Write the number as \(10t+u\) and its reversal as \(10u+t\) before translating either sentence.
The first fact reads \(10t+u=7(t+u)\), which becomes \(3t=6u\). Translate the second fact the same way, starting from \(10u+t=10t+u-18\).
review.sol: With \(t\) the tens digit and \(u\) the units digit, the number is \(10t+u\) and its reversal is \(10u+t\). The first fact reads \(10t+u=7(t+u)\), which simplifies to \(3t=6u\), so \(t=2u\). The second reads \(10u+t=10t+u-18\), which simplifies to \(t-u=2\). Then \(2u-u=2\) makes \(u=2\) and \(t=4\), so the number is \(\boxed{42}\). Both facts hold for 42, since \(7(4+2)=42\) and \(24=42-18\).

review.x: A canteen charges the same price for every roll and the same price for every bowl of soup. Three rolls and two bowls of soup cost 37 dollars, and five rolls and three bowls of soup cost 59 dollars. Enter the cost of four rolls and three bowls of soup, in dollars.
hints: No sentence gives a total number of items, so both facts are price facts. Name the price of a roll and the price of a bowl of soup, then write one equation per order.
Tripling \(3r+2s=37\) and doubling \(5r+3s=59\) both give \(6s\), so subtracting clears \(s\). Read the closing sentence again before typing.
review.sol: With \(r\) the price of a roll and \(s\) the price of a bowl of soup, \(3r+2s=37\) and \(5r+3s=59\). Tripling the first gives \(9r+6s=111\) and doubling the second gives \(10r+6s=118\), so subtracting leaves \(r=7\), and \(21+2s=37\) gives \(s=8\). Four rolls and three bowls of soup cost \(28+24=\boxed{52}\) dollars. Neither price is the answer, and the closing sentence names a third amount built from both.

review.x: Two trains leave stations 468 km apart at the same moment and travel toward each other at steady speeds, meeting 3 hours later. One train is 14 km per hour faster than the other. Enter how far the faster train traveled, in kilometers.
hints: Distance is rate times time, so in 3 hours each train covers 3 times its own rate, and the two distances add to 468 km.
Let \(x\) be the slower rate and \(y\) the faster, in km per hour. Then \(3x+3y=468\), and the second fact gives \(y=x+14\).
review.sol: With \(x\) the slower rate and \(y\) the faster, in km per hour, the two distances add to 468, so \(3x+3y=468\) and \(x+y=156\). The second fact is \(y=x+14\), so \(2x+14=156\), \(x=71\), and \(y=85\). The faster train travels \(3(85)=\boxed{255}\) km. The letters stand for rates and the question asks for a distance, so multiply the faster rate by the 3 hours.

review.x: A ticket window sells lawn seats at 18 dollars and pavilion seats at 32 dollars. One night it sold 11 fewer pavilion seats than lawn seats and took in 1898 dollars. Enter how much more money came from pavilion seats than from lawn seats, in dollars.
hints: The two unknowns are the seat counts, but the question asks for dollars, so find both counts first and multiply each count by its own price at the end.
Eleven fewer pavilion seats than lawn seats is \(P=L-11\). Substituting into \(18L+32P=1898\) gives \(50L-352=1898\).
review.sol: With \(L\) lawn seats and \(P\) pavilion seats, \(P=L-11\) and \(18L+32P=1898\), so \(18L+32(L-11)=1898\), giving \(50L=2250\) and \(L=45\), with \(P=34\). Pavilion money is \(32(34)=1088\) and lawn money is \(18(45)=810\), so the difference is \(\boxed{278}\) dollars. Neither 45 nor 34 is the answer, since each count still has to be multiplied by its own price before the subtraction.

blocks.x: Some stories name three quantities and state three facts, so the system has three letters and three equations. No new method is needed for that. One substitution, or one elimination, takes the count from three letters down to two, and 5.2 and 5.3 already solve what is left. The next two problems run that once, on one system.

The system \(x=4z+7\), \(2x+3y+5z=255\), and \(3x+y-2z=175\) has three letters, and the first equation is already solved for \(x\). Write \(4z+7\) in place of \(x\) in both of the other two, which leaves two equations in \(y\) and \(z\) alone. Solve that pair and enter \(z\).
hints: One equation is already solved for a letter, so \(4z+7\) can stand wherever \(x\) stands. Do the replacement in the second equation and in the third, not in just one of them.
After the replacement the second equation collects to \(3y+13z=241\) and the third to \(y+10z=154\). In \(y+10z=154\), \(y\) has coefficient \(1\).
blocks.sol: Substituting \(x=4z+7\) gives \(2(4z+7)+3y+5z=255\), which collects to \(3y+13z=241\), and \(3(4z+7)+y-2z=175\), which collects to \(y+10z=154\). From \(y+10z=154\), \(y=154-10z\), so \(3(154-10z)+13z=241\), then \(462-17z=241\) and \(17z=221\), so \(z=\boxed{13}\). Both replacements are needed, since doing only one leaves an equation that still carries \(x\) rather than a pair in \(y\) and \(z\).

blocks.x: Same system as the last problem, and \(z=13\) is now known. Find \(y\) and \(x\), then check the triple in all three original equations and enter \(x+y\).
hints: One of the two reduced equations is \(y+10z=154\), and with \(z\) known only \(y\) is left in it.
Neither reduced equation has an \(x\) in it, so \(x\) comes only from \(x=4z+7\), the equation that was already solved for it.
blocks.sol: \(y+10(13)=154\) gives \(y=24\), and \(x=4(13)+7=59\), so \(x+y=\boxed{83}\). The triple \((59,24,13)\) passes all three originals, \(59=4(13)+7\), \(118+72+65=255\), and \(177+24-26=175\). Two back-substitutions are needed, one for the second letter of the reduced pair and one for the letter that was replaced.

blocks.x: One substitution, one fewer letter. Solve one equation for one letter and write that expression in place of the letter in both of the other two equations. That removes the letter from both at once, and what is left is two equations in two letters, which 5.2 and 5.3 solve. Substituting into only one of them leaves two equations still carrying three letters, and two facts cannot pin three quantities. Back-substitution then runs twice, once into the reduced pair for its second letter and once into the equation that was solved, since that letter never appeared in the reduced pair.

In $$3x+4y+2z=150$$ $$5x+2y-2z=108$$ $$4x+3y+6z=231$$ no letter has coefficient \(1\) anywhere, so isolating one starts with a division. The \(z\)-terms are the cheap ones to match. Eliminate \(z\), once from the first and second equations and once from the first and third. Solve the two-letter system that comes out and enter \(x\).
hints: The \(z\)-terms are \(+2z\), \(-2z\) and \(+6z\). The first two are opposite already, and tripling the first equation matches the \(6z\) in the third.
Adding the first two equations leaves \(8x+6y=258\), and three times the first minus the third leaves \(5x+9y=219\). Every term of \(8x+6y=258\) divides by \(2\).
blocks.sol: Adding the first two equations clears \(z\) and gives \(8x+6y=258\), or \(4x+3y=129\). Three times the first equation minus the third gives \(5x+9y=219\). Tripling \(4x+3y=129\) gives \(12x+9y=387\), and subtracting leaves \(7x=168\), so \(x=\boxed{24}\). Then \(3y=129-96=33\) gives \(y=11\), and \(2z=150-72-44=34\) gives \(z=17\). Check in the third equation, \(96+33+102=231\).

blocks.x: Here is a system in three letters. $$5x+2y+3z=161$$ $$4x-2y+5z=55$$ $$3x+4y-2z=138$$ Clear \(y\) from two different pairs of equations, solve the two-letter system that is left, and enter \(y\).
hints: The \(y\)-terms are \(+2y\), \(-2y\) and \(+4y\). The first two are opposite already, and doubling the second equation makes \(-4y\), the opposite of the third's \(+4y\).
With those pairings the reduced pair is \(9x+8z=216\) and \(11x+8z=248\), both carrying \(8z\), so subtracting leaves \(x\) alone. The ask is \(y\), which appears in neither.
blocks.sol: Adding the first two equations gives \(9x+8z=216\). Adding twice the second equation to the third gives \(11x+8z=248\). Subtracting leaves \(2x=32\), so \(x=16\), then \(8z=216-144=72\) and \(z=9\). Back in the first equation, \(2y=161-80-27=54\), so \(y=\boxed{27}\). Check, \(4(16)-2(27)+5(9)=55\) and \(3(16)+4(27)-2(9)=138\). The letter cleared first is not in the reduced pair, so an original equation is the only place left to find its value.

blocks.x: Clear one letter from two different pairs. Pick one letter, eliminate it from one pair of the three equations and then from a different pair, and what is left is two equations in the other two letters. Combining the same pair a second way only rescales the equation already found, so the second line is a copy of the first and two letters are left with one fact between them. Which letter to clear is 5.3's cheapness question, asked across three coefficients instead of two. Check the finished triple in all three original equations, since a triple built from two of them need not fit the third.
